Issues.Title: [release/8.0] Fix HTTP/2 hang on reused streams when a window update races the final write
Issues.Body:
Backport of #69690 to release/8.0

/cc @halter73 @danield137

# Fix HTTP/2 hang on reused streams when a window update races the final write

Unschedule completed HTTP/2 producers before pooled streams are reused.

## Description

A stream WINDOW_UPDATE racing the final response write can leave an extra entry in Kestrel's HTTP/2 output queue. The writer discards that entry after the response completes without clearing the producer's `_isScheduled` flag. If the stream is pooled and reused, subsequent scheduling attempts return early and the new response is never sent.

Clear `_isScheduled` when dequeuing and skipping a completed producer. The completion check and flag update use the same lock as `Schedule()`. Preserve the existing scheduling token when the stream has already been reused. Include regression coverage for scheduling both after response completion and during the final write.

Fixes #53736

## Customer Impact

Intermittent HTTP/2 requests, including gRPC calls, can hang without receiving response headers while other requests on the same connection continue working. Larger responses can also leave server-side response writes blocked. Multiple customers have reported the issue, including after upgrading from .NET 6.

Increasing the client's initial HTTP/2 stream window can mitigate the issue for responses smaller than that window, but requires control of every affected client and is not a general server-side workaround.

## Regression?

- [x] Yes
- [ ] No

Regressed from .NET 6 in .NET 7 with #40925, which introduced the shared HTTP/2 output scheduling mechanism. The affected code remains in release/8.0.

## Risk

- [ ] High
- [ ] Medium
- [x] Low

The change is limited to the existing completed-producer discard path. It repairs scheduling bookkeeping without changing public APIs, normal response processing, or pooling policy. The previous completion-property check already acquired the same lock, so the change does not add a lock acquisition to each dequeue. The product patch is identical to the fix merged in #69690.

## Verification

- [x] Manual (required)
- [x] Automated

**Manual end-to-end:** Ran a standalone Kestrel h2c server and `SocketsHttpHandler` client over real loopback sockets on Windows x64, using the [64 KiB echo workload from the issue](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/53736#issuecomment-5958244396). Each run used 120,000 POST requests, 16 concurrent requests, one HTTP/2 connection, the default 65,535-byte initial client stream window, dynamic window sizing, and a five-second per-request timeout. No scheduling events were injected and no Kestrel state was modified at runtime. Successful responses were checked for HTTP/2, successful status, and byte-for-byte echo correctness.

- Without the writer-loop fix: **32 of 120,000 requests hung before receiving response headers**. All 32 reached the server handler with `_isScheduled` already true; it remained true and `_completedResponse` remained false when the requests timed out. The other 119,968 requests completed successfully on the same connection.
- With the fix: **0 hangs in 240,000 requests across two runs**. Every response body matched the request, all handlers completed, and server shutdown completed in both runs.

**Automated:** The original three regression cases in `Http2ConnectionTests` passed with the fix: `StreamPool_ScheduledAfterResponseCompleted_PooledStreamReusedAndResponseSent` (both `largeResponse` values) and `StreamPool_ScheduledDuringFinalWrite_PooledStreamReusedAndResponseSent`. Previously, all three cases timed out at the reused stream's response HEADERS without the fix in 33 runs each (99 individual executions).

</details>

## Packaging changes reviewed?

- [ ] Yes
- [ ] No
- [x] N/A

No packaging changes. Only two Kestrel implementation files and the existing functional-test file are changed.

# Clarify Blazor test proportionality and permanent regression test boundaries

<!-- Once all that is done, you're ready to go. Open the PR with the content below. -->

Clarify Blazor test-boundary proportionality in `src/Components/AGENTS.md` and `docs/BlazorComponentsGuidance.md`.

## Description

An audit of maintainer review feedback (`@kotlarmilos`) across 25 `agent-reviewed-approved` Blazor PRs identified a recurring source of agent-generated test and review bloat (10/25 PRs, including `#67406`, `#67663`, `#67716`, `#69827`, `#69871`, `#70081`, `#70084`, `#70112`, `#70299`, and `#70304`):

1. **Unnecessary Selenium E2E tests when a lower boundary faithfully owns the contract:** Wording in `src/Components/AGENTS.md` (`"The mandatory sample-to-E2E workflow"`, `"This does not waive E2E coverage required for shipped implementation work"`, and `"The fix remains blocked while Jest is its only regression proof"`) caused coding and review agents to add or demand heavyweight Selenium E2E tests + test-asset pages even when a focused `.NET` unit test or `Web.JS` `.test.ts` test completely and faithfully covered the changed contract.
2. **Multi-test control matrices on localized fixes:** The blanket instruction `"Include a nearest-opposite control, meaning the closest scenario that must remain green, and, when meaningful, an adjacent control driven by the same production producer"` caused agents to generate 3–6 standalone test methods for a 1–5 line fix instead of a single focused regression test (or extending an existing test/`[Theory]`).
3. **Test-only production hooks:** Agents occasionally introduced optional test-only parameters or hooks onto production methods (for example in `#67406`) instead of exercising existing entry points.

This PR updates `src/Components/AGENTS.md` (which is also projected into Blazor PR review bundles as the `permanent-regression-test-boundary` policy) and `docs/BlazorComponentsGuidance.md` to:
- Default to **one focused regression test** (or an additional assertion/`[Theory]` row in an existing test) at the smallest faithful owning boundary (`.NET` unit/integration test or `Web.JS` `.test.ts` test), reserving Selenium E2E tests for behaviors that genuinely depend on a real browser engine or cross-layer runtime integration.
- Require a nearest-opposite control assertion only when a fix narrows or flips a branch whose opposite path is not already covered by existing tests, and prefer asserting it inside the same test or `[Theory]` rather than creating a multi-test matrix.
- Prohibit adding test-only optional parameters, fields, properties, or hooks to production types when behavior can be exercised through existing entry points.
- Instruct PR reviewers not to ask for redundant Selenium E2E tests when a focused unit or `.test.ts` test already covers the contract, and to flag disproportionate test matrices or E2E scaffolding for consolidation.

### Validation

Issues.Title: Virtualize stops loading earlier variable-height items after appending and scrolling to the end
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I searched the existing issues.

The closest report I found is #69823, fixed by #69926 and backported in #70019. That report concerns an `ItemsProvider` load and stale correction undoing end pinning. #69926 also describes intermittent blank space while restoring an anchor, so this may be related. I did not find a report matching the in-memory append → `ScrollToItemAsync` → upward-scroll sequence below; I have not established whether the underlying cause is the same.

### Describe the bug

With `Virtualize<int>`, variable-height rows, and `AnchorMode.End`, scrolling upward after appending items while away from the end and then jumping to the last item can leave earlier items unrendered. The viewport exposes the leading spacer and can become completely blank.

The issue was first observed in an application and then reproduced in a standalone Blazor Server app containing only an in-memory list of integers and simple CSS. There is no `ItemsProvider`, backend service, or custom scrolling JavaScript.

### Reproduction

https://github.com/danroth27/BlazorVirtualizeEndAnchorRepro

With the .NET 11 SDK:

```powershell
dotnet run --launch-profile http --urls http://localhost:54187
```

1. Open `http://localhost:54187/?Overscan=5`.
2. Select **End of queue** under **Follow new entries**.
3. Move the list's scrollbar to approximately the middle and wait for rows to render.
4. Click **Add at end** nine times.
5. Click **Go to end**. This awaits `virtualizer.ScrollToItemAsync(items.Count - 1)`.
6. Scroll upward within the list, past the initially rendered tail. Approximately 6,000 pixels was sufficient in the tested run.

The list starts with 10,000 integers. Rows are 120 pixels tall, except every fifth row is 240 pixels tall. Appending replaces the list while retaining existing item identities, and each row has a stable `@key`.

### Expected behavior

Earlier items render as the viewport moves upward.

### Actual behavior

The rendered window can remain at the tail while scrolling exposes the leading spacer instead of earlier items.

In the latest overscan-5 run:

- Immediately after jumping: rendered items **9996–10009**, with four intersecting the viewport.
- After scrolling upward 6,000 pixels: still rendered items **9996–10009**, with **zero** intersecting the viewport.
- The list still contains all 10,009 items.

### Controls and timing

- Fixed-height rows worked in the tested control runs.
- Variable-height rows without appending before the jump worked in the tested control runs.
- A blank viewport also reproduced with overscan **15** in an earlier run, but not in every run. The latest default-15 run did not end with a fully blank viewport. Overscan 5 provides the more reliable reproduction.

These are observed results, not an assertion that the failure is limited to a particular overscan or that its precise cause is known.

### Environment

- .NET SDK: **11.0.100**
- ASP.NET Core runtime: **11.0.0**
- Target framework: **net11.0**
- OS: **Windows**
- Browser used for the isolated reproduction: **Microsoft Edge 157.0.0.0**, headless
- Rendering: **Blazor Server**, per-page interactivity

Issues.Title: Expose an API to explicitly refresh authentication for a Blazor Server circuit
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Provide a supported public API to explicitly refresh authentication for an active Blazor Server circuit, without reconnecting or reloading the page.

Blazor Server in .NET 11 consumes SignalR authentication refresh and enables automatic refresh on its underlying connection. However, applications don't have a first-class Blazor API to request a refresh immediately after obtaining updated credentials.

## Motivation

For example, an application can issue an updated authentication cookie through a separate HTTP request or another tab. The browser now has current credentials, but an existing circuit continues using its previous principal until its next authentication refresh.

An application that knows credentials have changed should be able to request reauthentication immediately, rather than shorten the scheduled refresh interval or reload the page and lose unsaved component state.

## Current workaround

SignalR exposes `HubConnection.refreshAuthentication()`, but Blazor owns the connection internally. Blazor's own authentication-refresh E2E tests capture the connection by wrapping the connection builder's `build()` method through `configureSignalR`, then invoke `refreshAuthentication()` on the captured connection.

Applications shouldn't need to intercept connection construction to access this capability.

- [Blazor test connection capture](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/release/11.0/src/Components/test/testassets/Components.TestServer/Pages/_ServerHost.cshtml)
- [Authentication-refresh E2E tests](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/release/11.0/src/Components/test/E2ETest/ServerExecutionTests/ServerAuthTest.cs)

## Requested capability

Expose an awaitable public API that:

- Requests authentication refresh through the existing SignalR mechanism using the browser's current credentials.
- Propagates the refreshed principal to the circuit's authentication state and dependent components without reconnecting or recreating the circuit.
- Reports completion and failures to the caller and respects the existing authentication-refresh security checks.

The exact JavaScript and/or C# API surface is open for design. For example, `Blazor.refreshAuthentication()` was raised in the original integration issue, but isn't currently exposed.

This request is about reauthenticating with credentials the application has already obtained. It does not include renewing credentials, automatically detecting database role changes, or bypassing security checks for identity transitions. Applications remain responsible for handling user-specific state appropriately when authentication changes.

## Related work

- #68170 implemented Blazor's consumption of SignalR authentication refresh and explicitly raised the question of a public refresh trigger. This issue tracks that remaining public API capability.
- #68284 addressed support for identity changes during authentication refresh.

Issues.Title: Add a format-agnostic, composable Blazor serialization contract
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Provide a static `BlazorSerializer` and `BlazorSerializerOptions` that let applications reuse an existing STJ serialization context or wire up third-party serializers for their own types. A provider receives the Blazor options and flows them into its own converter/formatter extensibility so it can call Blazor for framework values such as `ElementReference`, or for other types it does not handle.

The application keeps its typed model. It should not have to replace framework-typed properties with byte-array surrogates to make composition possible. The public boundary is opaque bytes, with byte-destination and bounded-input operations that do not require an intermediate owned array. Provider-specific framing and buffering remain the provider's responsibility.

For the initial implementation, keep System.Text.Json (STJ) as an internal implementation detail. Opaque byte-provider output is carried as Base64 binary values inside that internal JSON representation. STJ context-backed definitions can instead use the native JSON path without Base64 encoding. Both execution paths remain implementation details of the same format-agnostic contract. Unregistered application types keep the supported default behavior, and framework-owned serialization/deserialization cannot be overridden.

**Proposal:** The following scenarios and API-reference declarations describe the proposed contract. The exact signatures and provider adapter names are open for discussion, not existing APIs.

**JS interop is out of scope for this issue. We will make adjustments to this contract to support JS interop in follow-up work.** This proposal does not add serializer integration for JS invocations, object/stream references, or JavaScript-side codecs. The `ElementReference` example illustrates delegation to framework-owned serialization, not JS interop integration or reference portability across runtimes.

## Goals

1. **Wire up serializer providers.** Applications can reuse an existing STJ context or register MessagePack, protobuf-net, or another compatible provider for selected application/library types without exposing format-specific reader/writer APIs through the core contract or changing a process-global serializer configuration.

2. **Compose through the provider's native extensibility.** Providers receive the selected Blazor options and use those options from their own converter/formatter callbacks to serialize and deserialize framework values and externally handled child types. The normal application model retains its typed properties.

3. **Retain framework ownership.** Framework-owned values and component/state envelopes stay under Blazor's control in both directions. A provider delegates framework value handling rather than replacing its Blazor serialization contract.

4. **Preserve compatible and generated execution.** Ordinary upgrades retain supported defaults without additional AOT-related warnings or required changes. Generated/explicit definitions support configurations that cannot use reflection-based member discovery, while missing support fails clearly rather than silently using unsafe discovery or losing values.

## Non-goals

1. Integrate the contract with JS interop in this issue. Follow-up work will adjust the contract to support that integration.
2. Replace renderer, browser event, SignalR, WebView, or other host protocols with a third-party application format.
3. Let applications replace framework-owned serialization or make live references durable across unrelated runtimes.
4. Design each third-party serializer's field encoding, framing, buffer management, or format-specific edge cases. Those belong to its provider integration.

## Proposed solution

Applications configure `options.TypeInfoResolvers`. A provider resolver receives those options, supplies type definitions backed by its serializer, and makes the options available to native converters/formatters that need to call Blazor. The provider handles its selected outer types; Blazor handles protected framework children and selects any other delegated child definitions.

The configuration and type-definition model follows the familiar [STJ contract customization approach](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/serialization/system-text-json/custom-contracts), without exposing JSON-specific contracts.

For byte-backed providers, there are two distinct extension boundaries. The **Blazor-facing provider** reads/writes opaque bytes for a selected type. The **provider-native converter/formatter** participates in that serializer's ordinary traversal of a typed object and calls the static Blazor serializer for applicable members. This second boundary is what avoids requiring application-authored byte-array surrogates.

An application can also make its existing partial `JsonSerializerContext` implement `IBlazorTypeInfoResolver` and register the context directly. The application supplies that interface implementation. Blazor can internally recognize the registered context and wire its metadata directly into STJ, bypassing the application's forwarding byte-codec path and avoiding Base64. This is an internal optimization, not a second public registration contract.

The examples reuse STJ's existing source-generated context model, MessagePack formatter interfaces, and protobuf-net custom serializer interfaces. The Blazor interfaces, `MessagePackResolver`, `ProtobufNetResolver`, and the Blazor bridge adapters are proposed integrations, not existing APIs. JSON-specific types appear in the application's existing context, not in the format-agnostic core contract. The third-party examples do not imply that Blazor takes dependencies on those packages.

Configuration examples run before the first serialization/deserialization operation. Unless explicitly composing providers, the examples describe alternative configurations rather than additions to options that have already been finalized.

### Bridge Blazor definitions into internal STJ execution

Before `BlazorSerializer` starts an internal STJ serialization or deserialization operation, it obtains an STJ configuration with an internal `IJsonTypeInfoResolver` bridge over the selected `BlazorSerializerOptions.TypeInfoResolvers`. That configuration may be reused for the same finalized Blazor options; this is not process-global registration or mutation of options on every invocation. Applications register a provider once through Blazor, not separately with STJ.

The bridge applies Blazor's framework ownership and configured definition-selection rules before ordinary STJ handling can choose a conflicting generated or reflection-based contract. For a type `T` assigned to a byte provider, it supplies an internal `JsonTypeInfo<T>` backed by an internal `JsonConverter<T>`:

| Operation | Internal converter behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Write | Invoke the selected provider's byte codec for `T` and write its output as a Base64 JSON string. |
| Read | Decode the Base64 JSON string and invoke the selected provider's byte codec to reconstruct `T`. |

This applies to root values and nested properties alike. For example, an STJ-backed outer model containing a MessagePack-backed `CustomModel` must delegate that child to MessagePack rather than inspect its members through reflection. The outer model stays ordinary JSON; only the byte-provider child uses the Base64 carrier. Its codec still receives the selected Blazor options and can delegate its own children back to Blazor.

An STJ context-backed definition may use native generated metadata without a Base64 wrapper, but its traversal must still honor this bridge for nested provider-owned and framework-owned values. Merely appending another STJ resolver after a context that already supplies metadata for `T` is insufficient. The internal configuration must use compatible metadata and an execution path that honors the bridge, rather than blindly invoke a context's generated writer.

The converter invokes the already-selected byte codec; it does not recursively re-enter STJ for the same `T`. A provider failure is surfaced, not retried through reflection. Types left unhandled retain supported default behavior according to the selected reflection policy; configurations requiring generated/explicit support report missing definitions. The bridge must not introduce reflection-based member discovery for provider-owned types.

The STJ resolver, JSON converter, metadata adaptation and Base64 carrier remain internal implementation details. The public provider contract continues to expose opaque bytes and Blazor options, not STJ readers, writers or resolver interfaces.

## Scenarios and corresponding design

### 1. Wire up an STJ serializer using an existing context

An application already has a model and an STJ source-generated context. For example, its existing model is:

```csharp
public sealed class Report
{
    public int Revision { get; set; }

    public string Title { get; set; } = "";
}
```

Its existing [STJ context](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/serialization/system-text-json/source-generation) includes that model:

```csharp
[JsonSerializable(typeof(Report))]
internal partial class AppJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext
{
}
```

The application adds the Blazor resolver interface through another partial declaration and supplies its implementation. The following is API-reference notation: the application-written method body that adapts the context's generated metadata to Blazor definitions is omitted. Adding the interface alone is not sufficient, and Blazor does not generate this implementation:

```csharp
internal partial class AppJsonContext : IBlazorTypeInfoResolver
{
    BlazorTypeInfo? IBlazorTypeInfoResolver.GetTypeInfo(
        Type type, BlazorSerializerOptions options);
}
```

The application registers the context directly, without a separate STJ adapter object:

```csharp
var options = new BlazorSerializerOptions();
options.TypeInfoResolvers.Add(AppJsonContext.Default);
```

The model does not need new Blazor-specific annotations or a second set of generated serialization definitions. The application reuses its existing STJ context and provides the resolver integration.

The caller writes the value to its byte destination using the same options:

```csharp
BlazorSerializer.Serialize<Report>(destination, report, options);
```

The caller reads a corresponding bounded input using that configuration:

```csharp
Report restored =
    BlazorSerializer.Deserialize<Report>(input, options);
```

Here `destination` is an `IBufferWriter<byte>` and `input` is a `ReadOnlySequence<byte>`. The caller does not need to request an intermediate `byte[]` before writing or reading. This is a complete Blazor value, not a promise that its carrier can be passed directly to an STJ parser.

**Design flow:** The context satisfies the public Blazor resolver contract through the application's implementation. Internally, Blazor can recognize that this resolver is also a `JsonSerializerContext` and obtain its generated STJ metadata directly, rather than invoke the forwarding resolver/byte-codec path. Serialization and deserialization then use the normal internal JSON representation without a Base64 wrapper.

This native path still uses the internal STJ resolver bridge described above, so nested types assigned to another provider delegate to that provider instead of STJ's ordinary member discovery.

The optimization must preserve the resolver's intended type coverage, selection order and framework ownership rules. It is not permission to move contexts ahead of other registrations or bypass protected handling for nested framework values. The integration must also respect STJ metadata/options compatibility rather than mutate the existing context's read-only options.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Application
    participant B as BlazorSerializer
    participant C as Registered AppJsonContext
    participant J as STJ engine
    A->>B: Serialize Report with options
    B->>C: Resolve context metadata through internal fast path
    C-->>B: Generated Report metadata
    B->>J: Write JSON value directly using metadata
    J-->>B: Normal JSON representation without Base64
    B-->>A: Complete Blazor value
    A->>B: Deserialize Report with options
    B->>J: Read JSON value using context metadata
    J-->>B: Restored Report
    B-->>A: Restored Report
```

**Expected outcome:** The application reuses its existing STJ context in both directions without routing JSON through an opaque Base64 blob. If the context does not supply metadata for a type, context-based resolution declines that type rather than adding reflection-based discovery of its own. Other providers or supported defaults remain independently selectable. The public contract does not expose or require the internal STJ optimization.

### 2. Use native MessagePack formatters to delegate framework values

For a MessagePack-backed configuration, the application registers its provider:

```csharp
var options = new BlazorSerializerOptions();
options.TypeInfoResolvers.Add(new MessagePackResolver(options));
```

The application model keeps its `ElementReference` property:

```csharp
[MessagePackObject]
public sealed class Widget
{
    [Key(0)]
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";

    [Key(1)]
    public ElementReference Element { get; set; }
}
```

Application code uses the original typed model:

```csharp
BlazorSerializer.Serialize<Widget>(destination, widget, options);
```

The inverse operation restores the same model shape:

```csharp
Widget restored = BlazorSerializer.Deserialize<Widget>(input, options);
```

The provider author wires native MessagePack formatters that capture the supplied Blazor options. This uses MessagePack's existing [CompositeResolver mechanism](https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/blob/9bc353141d0a280b6a470f1db29d3e0790cbb8b4/src/MessagePack/Resolvers/CompositeResolver.cs); `applicationMessagePackResolver` supplies the provider's ordinary/generated model formatters:

```csharp
IFormatterResolver nativeResolver = CompositeResolver.Create(
    new IMessagePackFormatter[]
    {
        new BlazorMessagePackFormatter<ElementReference>(options)
    },
    new IFormatterResolver[] { applicationMessagePackResolver });
```

The provider uses that resolver in its own MessagePack configuration, not a process-global default:

```csharp
MessagePackSerializerOptions nativeOptions =
    MessagePackSerializerOptions.Standard.WithResolver(nativeResolver);
```

Its Blazor-delegating native formatter has the following proposed adapter declaration. The callbacks are MessagePack's existing [IMessagePackFormatter<T> interface](https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/blob/9bc353141d0a280b6a470f1db29d3e0790cbb8b4/src/MessagePack/Formatters/IMessagePackFormatter%601.cs); `_blazorOptions` is distinct from their `messagePackOptions` parameter:

```csharp
public sealed class BlazorMessagePackFormatter<T> : IMessagePackFormatter<T>
{
    private readonly BlazorSerializerOptions _blazorOptions;

    public BlazorMessagePackFormatter(BlazorSerializerOptions options);

    public void Serialize(
        ref MessagePackWriter writer, T value,
        MessagePackSerializerOptions messagePackOptions);

    public T Deserialize(
        ref MessagePackReader reader,
        MessagePackSerializerOptions messagePackOptions);
}
```

From its serialization callback, the formatter delegates `T` to Blazor using the captured options:

```csharp
BlazorSerializer.Serialize<T>(fieldDestination, value, _blazorOptions);
```

From its deserialization callback, it delegates the corresponding bounded field input:

```csharp
T restored = BlazorSerializer.Deserialize<T>(fieldInput, _blazorOptions);
```

`fieldDestination` and `fieldInput` are the provider's compatible byte boundary for that native field. They are not invented MessagePack methods or casts of `MessagePackWriter`. Adapting the native field to that boundary is the provider's responsibility. The Blazor contract does not force an owned array, but it does not promise that every third-party field can be written without buffering.

**Design flow:** MessagePack traverses `Widget` normally. On its `Element` member, the provider-installed native formatter calls Blazor with the options originally supplied to `MessagePackResolver`. Blazor uses the protected framework definition; the native formatter embeds or reads the resulting opaque child value without knowing its encoding.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as BlazorSerializer
    participant M as MessagePack engine
    participant F as Provider native formatter
    participant P as Protected framework handling
    B->>M: Serialize original typed Widget
    M->>F: Serialize Element member
    F->>B: Serialize T with captured Blazor options
    B->>P: Framework-owned serialization
    P-->>F: Opaque child value
    F-->>M: Valid native member representation
    M->>F: Deserialize that member
    F->>B: Deserialize T with captured options
    B->>P: Framework-owned reconstruction
    P-->>F: Typed framework value
    F-->>M: Restored member
```

**Expected outcome:** No application `WidgetPacket`, `ByteString` mapping, or byte-array property is required. Blazor, not the MessagePack formatter, controls the framework value's encoding and reconstruction. The appropriate host context and supported lifetime rules still apply; options alone do not establish that context. The provider also supplies any native generated formatter/analyzer metadata required by its chosen configuration.

### 3. Use a different provider's native custom serializer mechanism

The same Blazor capability applies to a Protocol Buffers implementation with native custom serializer extensibility, such as protobuf-net:

```csharp
options.TypeInfoResolvers.Add(new ProtobufNetResolver(options));
```

protobuf-net exposes [ISerializer<T>](https://github.com/protobuf-net/protobuf-net/blob/521ad0bff9a02e1ba7fb81bea322e790ddc89162/src/protobuf-net.Core/Serializers/IProtoSerializerT.cs) with native reader/writer callbacks. A provider's bridge can use this shape:

```csharp
public sealed class BlazorProtobufNetSerializer<T> : ISerializer<T>
{
    public SerializerFeatures Features { get; }
    public void Write(ref ProtoWriter.State state, T value);
    public T Read(ref ProtoReader.State state, T value);
}
```

The provider makes its supplied Blazor options available to those native callbacks through a mechanism supported by that engine. From there, it uses the same static Blazor byte operations shown in scenario 2 for the applicable `T`.

**Design flow:** The provider owns native registration, options flow, and field adaptation. Blazor's requirement is that those callbacks can use the provided options to delegate a framework value or another externally handled type. The exact protobuf-net adapter is not established by this declaration, and this feature does not prescribe its framing algorithms or context plumbing.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant R as ProtobufNetResolver
    participant N as Native protobuf-net serializer
    participant B as BlazorSerializer
    participant F as Protected framework handling
    R->>N: Supply native integration and Blazor options
    N->>B: Write delegated T with provided options
    B->>F: Select framework definition when applicable
    F-->>N: Opaque bytes
    N->>B: Read delegated T with provided options
    B->>F: Reconstruct framework value
    F-->>N: Typed value
```

**Expected outcome:** The integration uses a provider's converter/serializer hooks, rather than requiring application-authored binary surrogate properties. This example refers to protobuf-net, not a claim that Google's generated `.proto` classes expose the same CLR converter mechanism. Providers that need a surrogate may still use one.

### 4. Compose providers and delegate other application/library types

A library and an application contribute their own definitions to the same selected configuration:

```csharp
options.TypeInfoResolvers.Add(new ApplicationResolver(options));
options.TypeInfoResolvers.Add(new MessagePackResolver(options));
```

A provider-native formatter can delegate a child type it does not handle, just as it delegates a framework value:

```csharp
BlazorSerializer.Serialize<TChild>(fieldDestination, child, _blazorOptions);
```

The matching read uses the same captured configuration:

```csharp
TChild child =
    BlazorSerializer.Deserialize<TChild>(fieldInput, _blazorOptions);
```

**Design flow:** Blazor selects the child's framework, application, library or default definition. A provider claims only supported roots; delegating the same unsupported root back to the same selected provider indefinitely is not a fallback mechanism. Explicit resolver order makes selection deterministic without a process-global registration pass.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant N as Native provider callback
    participant B as BlazorSerializer
    participant O as BlazorSerializerOptions
    participant C as Selected child definition
    N->>B: Serialize or deserialize TChild with supplied options
    B->>O: Resolve child under framework ownership rules
    O-->>B: Child definition
    B->>C: Execute matching byte operation
    C-->>N: Child bytes or typed value
```

**Expected outcome:** A provider does not need to know another library's implementation. It must not replace the supplied options with private defaults. Capturing provider instances and their native formatter caches belong to that options configuration, not a process-global cache keyed only by type.

### 5. Preserve framework ownership and supported default behavior

An unregistered application type continues to use supported default handling:

```csharp
BlazorSerializer.Serialize<Person>(destination, person, options);
```

The corresponding read uses that default contract:

```csharp
Person restored = BlazorSerializer.Deserialize<Person>(input, options);
```

This assumes the configured providers do not claim `Person`. Framework-owned values and component/state envelopes retain their framework-defined handling. Provider resolver order and type definitions cannot replace Blazor's protected contracts.

**Design flow:** Protected framework lookup precedes application resolver selection in both directions, including nested calls. Non-framework types use the selected provider or supported defaults.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Consumer or native callback
    participant B as BlazorSerializer
    participant F as Protected framework handling
    participant A as Application definitions
    C->>B: Read or write selected value
    alt Framework-owned value
        B->>F: Use protected contract
        F-->>C: Framework result or supported failure
    else Application value
        B->>A: Use provider or supported default
        A-->>C: Value or bytes
    end
```

**Expected outcome:** Ordinary upgrades do not opt all application values into blobs or require new AOT changes. Configurations that require generated/explicit support report missing/unsupported definitions clearly. Runtime `Type` lookup may select an available definition; it is not itself unsafe member discovery.

Descriptor consumers retain concrete runtime parameter selection, such as an `Employee` value passed to a `Person` parameter, without surrendering the descriptor envelope. Adoption by component-descriptor and persistence consumers can be delivered separately while preserving their existing lifecycle and storage obligations. This proposal defines the shared contract rather than redesigning those consumers.

## Design overview and proposed primitives

The core abstraction is a type definition with matching serialization/deserialization behavior. Byte-provider definitions use the public byte codec contract and configure their native child extensibility with the Blazor options. Internally, Blazor may execute a registered STJ context directly instead of invoking that context's application-provided forwarding implementation. The static serializer performs selection and framework ownership checks; providers never receive a public STJ writer/reader.

```mermaid
graph TD
    App["Application"] --> Options["BlazorSerializerOptions"]
    Options --> Resolver["Provider type-info resolver"]
    Serializer["Static BlazorSerializer"] --> Options
    Serializer --> Context["Registered STJ context"]
    Context --> Native["Native STJ path (internal)"]
    Resolver --> Codec["Provider byte codec"]
    Codec --> Engine["Native third-party serializer"]
    Engine --> Formatter["Provider-native converter or formatter"]
    Formatter --> Serializer
    Serializer --> Bridge["Internal STJ resolver bridge"]
    Bridge --> Resolver
    Bridge --> Framework
    Serializer --> Framework["Protected framework handling"]
    Native --> Framework
```

The following are API-reference declarations, not implementations. Runtime/host binding and final package placement remain open; the proposed namespace is `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Serialization`. The sample provider classes belong to their provider packages, not to Blazor.

### Static serializer

Buffer-oriented operations are the primary composition path:

```csharp
public static class BlazorSerializer
{
    public static void Serialize<T>(
        IBufferWriter<byte> destination, T value,
        BlazorSerializerOptions options);

    public static void Serialize(
        IBufferWriter<byte> destination, object? value,
        Type type, BlazorSerializerOptions options);

    public static T Deserialize<T>(
        ReadOnlySequence<byte> input, BlazorSerializerOptions options);

    public static object? Deserialize(
        ReadOnlySequence<byte> input, Type type,
        BlazorSerializerOptions options);
}
```

Array/span convenience overloads can be added without making an intermediate array a provider requirement. The framework owns the distinction between a complete Blazor-encoded value and a provider's raw codec bytes.

### Options and resolver registration

There is one primary registration path:

```csharp
public sealed class BlazorSerializerOptions
{
    public BlazorSerializerOptions();
    public IList<IBlazorTypeInfoResolver> TypeInfoResolvers { get; }
    public bool IsReadOnly { get; }
    public void MakeReadOnly();
    public BlazorTypeInfo GetTypeInfo(Type type);
}
```

Configuration is mutable until finalization/first use. Provider construction must not freeze the still-configuring options. Capturing providers are constructed for their owner; a shallow copy that leaves them pointing at different original options is not part of this proposal.

### Type-info resolver

A resolver selects definitions; it does not serialize a value during lookup:

```csharp
public interface IBlazorTypeInfoResolver
{
    BlazorTypeInfo? GetTypeInfo(
        Type type, BlazorSerializerOptions options);
}
```

Returning no definition means the resolver does not handle that type. Generated/library resolvers can supply precomputed closed definitions without arbitrary runtime generic construction.

### Provider resolver declaration

The STJ example uses the application's existing context and its application-provided interface implementation from scenario 1. No separate public STJ resolver adapter is required.

The proposed MessagePack integration captures options and supplies matching definitions:

```csharp
public sealed class MessagePackResolver : IBlazorTypeInfoResolver
{
    public MessagePackResolver(BlazorSerializerOptions options);
    public BlazorTypeInfo? GetTypeInfo(
        Type type, BlazorSerializerOptions options);
}
```

The protobuf-net provider participates through the same Blazor-facing contract:

```csharp
public sealed class ProtobufNetResolver : IBlazorTypeInfoResolver
{
    public ProtobufNetResolver(BlazorSerializerOptions options);
    public BlazorTypeInfo? GetTypeInfo(
        Type type, BlazorSerializerOptions options);
}
```

### Byte codec identity

The non-generic base identifies the represented type; supported external implementation uses its generic form:

```csharp
public abstract class BlazorConverter
{
    protected BlazorConverter();
    public abstract Type Type { get; }
}
```

### Typed byte codec

This is the provider's outer Blazor byte boundary, distinct from its engine-native child callbacks:

```csharp
public abstract class BlazorConverter<T> : BlazorConverter
{
    protected BlazorConverter();
    public sealed override Type Type { get; }

    public abstract void Write(
        IBufferWriter<byte> destination, T value,
        BlazorSerializerOptions options);

    public abstract T Read(
        ReadOnlySequence<byte> input,
        BlazorSerializerOptions options);
}
```

`Write` produces the provider's raw bytes; `Read` receives those bytes after Blazor removes its carrier. The generic base supplies the framework's internal erased dispatch bridge. It does not expose a JSON token contract or require the application to construct reflected adapters.

### Type definition

A byte-backed definition keeps a type and its matching read/write codec together:

```csharp
public abstract class BlazorTypeInfo
{
    private protected BlazorTypeInfo();
    public Type Type { get; }
    public BlazorConverter Converter { get; }
}
```

The typed form constrains the codec at construction:

```csharp
public sealed class BlazorTypeInfo<T> : BlazorTypeInfo
{
    public BlazorTypeInfo(BlazorConverter<T> converter);
}
```

These declarations describe the public byte-provider contract. Internal native STJ execution does not require the application to use a different public metadata type or expose JSON readers/writers. There is no public property-graph customization model required by these declarations. An application-provided definition cannot bypass protected framework lookup.

### Dependency map

```mermaid
classDiagram
    BlazorSerializer --> BlazorSerializerOptions
    BlazorSerializerOptions --> IBlazorTypeInfoResolver
    IBlazorTypeInfoResolver --> BlazorTypeInfo
    BlazorTypeInfo --> BlazorConverter
    BlazorConverterT --|> BlazorConverter
    BlazorTypeInfoT --|> BlazorTypeInfo
    BlazorTypeInfoT --> BlazorConverterT
    AppJsonContext ..|> IBlazorTypeInfoResolver
    AppJsonContext --|> JsonSerializerContext
    BlazorSerializer ..> JsonSerializerContext : internal recognition
    MessagePackResolver ..|> IBlazorTypeInfoResolver
    ProtobufNetResolver ..|> IBlazorTypeInfoResolver
    MessagePackResolver --> BlazorSerializerOptions
    MessagePackResolver --> BlazorMessagePackFormatterT
    BlazorMessagePackFormatterT --> BlazorSerializer
```

Names ending in `T` are aliases for the generic declarations, not extra types. Native engines and existing framework handlers are integration participants, not new public Blazor abstractions. Existing consumer signatures are not changed by this provider-facing proposal.

Issues.Title: FieldIdentifier.Create throws ArgumentException when an indexer argument is a captured long, Guid or other non-int value type
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

`FieldIdentifier.Create` throws when the accessor indexes a collection with a **captured** value-type argument other than `int`, for example `() => byLong[key]` where `key` is a `long` local or field. The same happens for `Guid`, `DateTime` and any other value type that implements `ISpanFormattable` or `IFormattable`.

In a Blazor app this means an input bound with `@bind-Value="byLong[key]"` (including the built-in `InputText`) throws while rendering.

`int`, `string` and constant arguments (`byLong[1L]`) work.

Cause: in `src/Components/Shared/src/ExpressionFormatting/ExpressionFormatter.cs`, `CreateCapturedValueFormatter` calls `CompileMemberEvaluator<ISpanFormattable>` (or `<IFormattable>`) for these types. `CompileMemberEvaluator<TResult>` builds `Expression.Lambda<Func<object, TResult>>` directly on the member expression, whose type is the value type, so `Expression.Lambda` rejects it: the value is never boxed. The code is the same on `main` and `release/10.0`.

### Expected Behavior

`FieldIdentifier.Create(() => byLong[key])` returns a `FieldIdentifier` with `FieldName` = the formatted key (`"1"`), as it does for an `int` key or a constant `long` key.

### Steps To Reproduce

Save as `repro.cs` and run `dotnet run repro.cs` (.NET 10 SDK):

```csharp
#:sdk Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Forms;

var byInt = new Dictionary<int, string> { [1] = "a" };
var byLong = new Dictionary<long, string> { [1] = "a" };
var byGuid = new Dictionary<Guid, string> { [Guid.Empty] = "a" };
int i = 1; long l = 1; var g = Guid.Empty;

Run("dict[capturedInt]", () => FieldIdentifier.Create(() => byInt[i]));
Run("dict[capturedLong]", () => FieldIdentifier.Create(() => byLong[l]));
Run("dict[capturedGuid]", () => FieldIdentifier.Create(() => byGuid[g]));
Run("dict[1L] (constant)", () => FieldIdentifier.Create(() => byLong[1L]));

static void Run(string name, Func<FieldIdentifier> create)
{
    try { var f = create(); Console.WriteLine($"{name,-22} OK   FieldName={f.FieldName}"); }
    catch (Exception ex) { Console.WriteLine($"{name,-22} FAIL {ex.GetType().Name}: {ex.Message}"); }
}
```

Output:

```
dict[capturedInt]      OK   FieldName=1
dict[capturedLong]     FAIL ArgumentException: Expression of type 'System.Int64' cannot be used for return type 'System.ISpanFormattable'
dict[capturedGuid]     FAIL ArgumentException: Expression of type 'System.Guid' cannot be used for return type 'System.ISpanFormattable'
dict[1L] (constant)    OK   FieldName=1
```

The same in a component: `<InputText @bind-Value="byLong[key]" />` with `private long key = 1;` throws on render.

### Exceptions (if any)

```
System.ArgumentException: Expression of type 'System.Int64' cannot be used for return type 'System.ISpanFormattable'
   at System.Linq.Expressions.Expression.ValidateLambdaArgs(Type delegateType, Expression& body, ReadOnlyCollection`1 parameters, String paramName)
   at System.Linq.Expressions.Expression.Lambda[TDelegate](Expression body, String name, Boolean tailCall, IEnumerable`1 parameters)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Forms.ExpressionFormatter.<CreateCapturedValueFormatter>g__CompileMemberEvaluator|13_0[TResult](MemberExpression memberExpression)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Forms.ExpressionFormatter.CreateCapturedValueFormatter(MemberExpression memberExpression)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Forms.ExpressionFormatter.FormatCapturedValue(MemberExpression memberExpression, ConstantExpression constantExpression, ReverseStringBuilder& builder)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Forms.ExpressionFormatter.FormatIndexArgument(Expression indexExpression)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Forms.FieldIdentifier.ParseAccessor[T](Expression`1 accessor, Object& model, String& fieldName)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Forms.FieldIdentifier.Create[TField](Expression`1 accessor)
```

### .NET Version

10.0.403 (runtime 10.0.14); also 11.0.100-rc.2

### Anything else?

Tested:

| Runtime | PublishAot | captured `long` / `Guid` |
|---|---|---|
| .NET 10.0.14 | false | throws |
| .NET 10.0.14 | true (run with `dotnet run`) | throws |
| .NET 11.0 RC2 | false | throws |
| .NET 11.0 RC2 | true | works (the `!RuntimeFeature.IsDynamicCodeSupported` reflection path added in #68307) |

Suggested fix: convert the member expression to `TResult` before building the lambda:

```csharp
Expression body = memberExpression.Update(convertExpression);
if (body.Type != typeof(TResult))
{
    body = Expression.Convert(body, typeof(TResult));
}

var replacedExpression = Expression.Lambda<Func<object, TResult>>(body, parameterExpression);
```

- OS: macOS (arm64)

Issues.Title: Introduce generated binding-target metadata for Blazor forms
Issues.Body:
# Summary

This document proposes adding generated binding-target metadata to Blazor forms to remove runtime expression-tree inspection, reflected member access, and expression compilation from supported Native AOT/full-trimming form scenarios. Inputs, labels, validation messages, and nested editors use that metadata to preserve field identity, indexed paths, supported names, and localized display information while leaving value delivery, callbacks, and input editing behavior unchanged.

Razor supplies a non-generic BindMetadata through the bound parameter's companion metadata parameter: ValueMetadata for Value, following the Value/ValueExpression/ValueMetadata naming convention. Existing applications retain their supported expression-based experience without new warnings or mandatory AOT-related changes when upgrading without enabling additional AOT features or checks.

## Goals

1. **Identify fields without runtime expression processing.** Supported generated form scenarios must obtain field owner/member identity and full paths without framework reflection discovery/invocation or runtime-code-generation fallbacks in strict Native AOT/full-trimming execution.

2. **Preserve metadata semantics across consumers.** Inputs, labels, validation messages, custom inputs, and nested editors must agree on field identity and names, including supported indexes, naming overrides, display attributes, localization, and explicit overrides.

3. **Keep metadata independent from editing.** Existing Value/ValueChanged callbacks, synchronous/asynchronous setters, after-callbacks, input-local state, and validation notifications retain their behavior. Metadata does not read or assign the final bound value.

4. **Preserve ordinary upgrades and diagnose strict gaps.** Supported generated scenarios publish without trimming or ILC warnings caused by these metadata paths. Non-opt-in upgrades introduce no additional warnings or required AOT-related code/configuration/accessibility changes; strict unsupported cases produce actionable diagnostics rather than silent fallbacks.

## Non-goals

**Value access and assignment through BindMetadata.** The metadata contract does not add final-value getters or setters. Existing Value and ValueChanged delivery already provides those capabilities; adding them to BindMetadata would expand the contract beyond the metadata its consumers need.

## Proposed solution

Provide a metadata capability distinct from the existing typed value and callback contracts:

```csharp
public abstract class BindMetadata
{
    public abstract object GetOwner();
    public abstract string GetMemberName();
    public abstract string GetFieldPath();
    public abstract string? GetDisplayName();
}
```

Applicable components opt into metadata by declaring a companion [Parameter] named <BoundParameterName>Metadata. For a Value parameter, the declaration is:

```csharp
[Parameter]
public BindMetadata? ValueMetadata { get; set; }
```

For @bind-Value, Razor recognizes the declared ValueMetadata parameter and supplies the generated BindMetadata to it. The convention follows the bound parameter name rather than a fixed metadata parameter name: @bind-SelectedItem uses SelectedItemMetadata when that companion [Parameter] is declared. Components without a matching metadata parameter are not passed an undeclared parameter. ValueChanged remains the callback companion and ValueExpression remains the existing expression companion; metadata/expression coexistence is a separate open decision.

These are API proposals, not approved declarations. A consumer that requires target metadata must obtain valid metadata or its supported compatibility equivalent; nullable parameter syntax does not authorize silently missing field identity.

GetOwner and GetMemberName identify the field using owner reference identity and the member-name string. GetFieldPath supplies the binding path independently of that identity and without an enclosing editor prefix. GetDisplayName resolves supported localized metadata or returns null for consumer fallback. Explicit consumer overrides retain their supported precedence.

Razor supplies the required target metadata for supported binding shapes, including evaluated indexes. A concrete bound value type is unnecessary when the declared member shape is already known. Generation is shared across .razor/.cs inputs and composes library and application contributions.

### Bind a model property

Before and after adoption, the application writes:

```razor
<InputText @bind-Value="customer.Name" />
```

The input receives the existing value/callback and generated metadata identifying customer as owner, "Name" as member, and "customer.Name" as path. Metadata resolution does not evaluate the final Name value or replace the input's editing/callback flow.

### Identify nested fields and repeated model references

```razor
<InputText @bind-Value="customer.Address.City" />
<InputText @bind-Value="selectedAddress.City" />
```

This preserves existing Blazor FieldIdentifier semantics. The first target's identity is the Address instance and "City", not the component and the full path. If selectedAddress is that same instance, both targets produce equal FieldIdentifier values because their owner references and field-name strings match, even though their paths differ. Equal-but-distinct model objects do not become the same field. The owner must be a reference type; the field value itself can be a value type.

### Identify indexed fields

```razor
<InputNumber @bind-Value="customer.Orders[index].Total" />
```

For captured index 3, owner/member identify the selected order and "Total", while the path is "customer.Orders[3].Total". Supported array and single-argument indexer targets preserve consistent index evaluation between identity and path.

For a terminal target customer.Orders[index], owner is the collection and member name is the formatted index, not the full path. Supported index formatting and member naming behavior must be retained. Exact capture/refresh behavior when indexes, model references, or component parameters change remains an explicit design decision.

### Use metadata in generic components

```razor
@typeparam TValue

<InputSelect TValue="TValue" @bind-Value="localValue" />

@code {
    private TValue localValue = default!;
}
```

The wrapper's declared localValue member is known even while TValue is open. Generated metadata can identify the wrapper instance and "localValue" without knowing the concrete TValue.

### Resolve display names and explicit overrides

```razor
<InputNumber @bind-Value="customer.Age" DisplayName="Age in years" />
```

The input's explicit DisplayName retains precedence over generated display metadata. Without an explicit override, a supported DisplayAttribute name takes precedence over DisplayNameAttribute; absent supported display metadata returns null and the consumer uses its existing fallback, such as the field's member name.

Localized names must remain correct for the relevant CurrentUICulture. A generated string snapshot must not silently replace supported culture-dependent resolution. Supported annotation/resource-access details and consumer cache behavior across culture changes remain to be finalized without runtime attribute discovery.

### Integrate labels and validation messages

Existing applications can write:

```razor
<Label For="() => customer.Name" />
<InputText @bind-Value="customer.Name" />
<ValidationMessage For="() => customer.Name" />
```

Inputs and messages use the same owner/member identity. Non-wrapping labels preserve the appropriate input-id association; wrapping labels retain their child-content behavior. Static form names and validation-message targets use the correctly prefixed path, while interactive validation still selects messages by field identity.

The exact metadata entry point/compiler treatment for For remains open. This scenario states the required consumer outcome and existing syntax, not a claim that arbitrary expression instances can already execute through the strict path.

### Compose nested editors and explicit names

```razor
<AddressEditor @bind-Value="customer.Address" />
```

An AddressEditor using Editor<Address> and editing Value.City retains the enclosing path relationship, producing the appropriate customer.Address.City name rather than duplicating "Value" or discarding the prefix. Prefix composition occurs outside BindMetadata and must not change the actual field owner/member pair.

Existing explicit name/id overrides retain their supported consumer precedence. Editor.NameFor and other expression-based helper integration must be addressed with the explicit-expression compatibility contract rather than left on a silent strict reflection fallback.

### Adopt metadata in custom inputs and wrappers

A custom input opts into compiler-supplied metadata by exposing ValueMetadata alongside its existing Value and ValueChanged parameters and uses the owner/member pair to construct a FieldIdentifier. It retains control of parsing messages, input-local state, callback invocation, and EditContext notifications.

```csharp
[Parameter]
public BindMetadata? ValueMetadata { get; set; }
```

An input wrapper must distinguish metadata for its own local member from metadata forwarded for the outer model target. The feature must provide a supported adoption path for custom components without assuming every existing component automatically accepts the new parameter; forwarding and expression/metadata coexistence rules remain open.

### Identify a field from component code

A custom input or other component receiving ValueMetadata can construct a FieldIdentifier without inspecting an expression:

```csharp
FieldIdentifier field = new(
    ValueMetadata.GetOwner(),
    ValueMetadata.GetMemberName());
```

Application code that already knows the owner and member can continue using the existing constructor directly:

```csharp
FieldIdentifier field = new(customer, nameof(Customer.Name));
```

Neither operation needs expression processing. Existing expression-based calls remain supported through the reflection-compatible experience:

```csharp
FieldIdentifier field = FieldIdentifier.Create(() => customer.Name);
```

This feature does not automatically transform that C# call into generated metadata. The remaining API question is how callers that need the full metadata capability, rather than only a FieldIdentifier, request generated metadata outside a component @bind. This includes explicit For and ValueExpression consumers.

### Encapsulate the reflection compatibility path

When generated metadata is not supplied, the supported expression-based compatibility path can create BindMetadata through the proposed factory:

```csharp
public static BindMetadata Create<TValue>(
    Expression<Func<TValue>> expression);
```

This is the reflection path: it encapsulates existing expression processing and reflected metadata access behind the same contract used by generated metadata. Consumers use the supplied metadata when available; otherwise, compatibility execution adapts its existing expression through this factory. Exact trimming annotations and factory integration remain subject to design and API review.

The factory preserves existing expression limitations and evaluation failures. Expressions such as () => CalculateTotal() do not identify a supported field; null owners, invalid indexes, and value-type owners retain the applicable existing failure behavior. These are unsupported expressions or target-evaluation failures, not an additional category of invalid generated metadata.

Strict execution must not silently enter this reflection path when required generated metadata is missing. Its explicit-expression integration and actionable diagnostics remain to be defined.

### Upgrade without additional AOT opt-in

Applications upgrading without enabling extra AOT features or checks retain their supported components, expression parameters, custom input behavior, and build/publish diagnostics. Strict metadata generation does not impose mandatory new declarations on that compatibility path.
