Issues.Title: Make Blazor attribute binding conversion Native AOT and trimming compatible
Issues.Body:
# Summary

This feature enables Blazor attribute binding conversion to work with Native AOT and full trimming without runtime converter discovery or dynamically constructed conversion code. It preserves supported formatting, parsing, callbacks, input-local state, and conversion-related validation behavior.

Razor favors statically selected conversion whenever the required type and conversion are known. Framework conversion handles common types and enums; known custom converters are referenced directly. When generic code needs custom conversion, a fixed cascading value supplies the appropriate converter through a typed carrier. Applications that do not enable additional AOT features or checks retain their supported experience without new warnings or required changes.

## Goals

1. **Support concrete and generic conversion without runtime discovery.** Element bindings and input components handle supported scalar, enum, nullable, array, and custom-converter values without framework runtime converter discovery or reflected generic construction in strict execution. A generic component can originate a binding to its own state without receiving a parent-facing converter parameter.

2. **Preserve binding and input behavior.** Supported culture, formatting, null/empty values, invalid input, synchronous/asynchronous setters, after-callbacks, input-local state, and EditContext notifications retain their existing semantics. Supplying a converter does not bypass the input's established editing and validation behavior.

3. **Provide a strict path without degrading ordinary upgrades.** Supported conversion scenarios publish without trimming or ILC warnings attributable to these framework paths and execute without reflection fallbacks. Upgrading without opting into additional AOT features or checks adds no warnings or required AOT-related code, accessibility, or configuration changes.

## Non-goals

**Expanding the set of supported conversions.** Framework conversion and statically supplied custom converters cover the existing conversion surface; adding conversions for previously unsupported types is not part of this feature.

## Proposed solution

Extend BindConverter and the binding callback factory so known conversions can be selected directly and custom TypeConverter instances can be supplied explicitly. No new generic conversion interface is required. Existing Value and ValueChanged delivery remains responsible for ordinary component binding; forwarding a typed value alone does not require attribute conversion.

The selection model has two paths:

1. **Statically known conversion.** Razor uses framework conversion for supported known types or directly references the converter associated with a known custom type. Reusable conversion logic is not generated anew for every binding.
2. **Generic resolution when needed.** Framework conversion handles supported built-in and enum cases without custom discovery. A generic consumer that needs a custom converter receives it through a fixed cascading value, typed by the target value type.

Custom converter associations come from compiler-visible declarations such as TypeConverterAttribute. Library and application definitions make the required converters available ahead of time, including statically established generic usages. The selected application's definitions determine availability; parents do not manually pass a converter through every component layer.

BindConverter owns binding-specific formatting/parsing, including Boolean attribute behavior and supported array/nullable handling. EventCallback.Factory.CreateBinder continues to return EventCallback<ChangeEventArgs> and retains assignment, empty-input, and synchronous/asynchronous callback behavior. Culture and format remain operation arguments, not mutable settings on a shared carrier.

The following APIs and lowering examples are proposals, not implemented behavior or API-approved signatures. Lowering is included with its scenario; qualification, sequence numbers, and unrelated generated code are simplified.

### Bind a text value or a checkbox

Before and after adoption, the application writes the same Razor:

```razor
<input @bind="customer.Name" />
<input type="checkbox" @bind="customer.IsActive" />
```

For these known framework types, Razor uses direct framework conversion without introducing a cascading property or constructing a converter per binding. The text binding has this lowering shape:

```csharp
builder.OpenElement(0, "input");
builder.AddAttribute(1, "value", BindConverter.FormatValue(customer.Name));
builder.AddAttribute(2, "onchange",
    EventCallback.Factory.CreateBinder(
        this, __value => customer.Name = __value, customer.Name));
builder.SetUpdatesAttributeName("value");
builder.CloseElement();
```

The checkbox binding preserves Boolean checked values:

```csharp
builder.OpenElement(0, "input");
builder.AddAttribute(1, "type", "checkbox");
builder.AddAttribute(2, "checked", BindConverter.FormatValue(customer.IsActive));
builder.AddAttribute(3, "onchange",
    EventCallback.Factory.CreateBinder(
        this, __value => customer.IsActive = __value, customer.IsActive));
builder.SetUpdatesAttributeName("checked");
builder.CloseElement();
```

False remains a Boolean conditional attribute value, not the truthy text "false". These framework paths must not acquire broad preservation requirements merely because BindConverter also supports custom types.

### Preserve culture, formatting, and callbacks

```razor
<input @bind="amount" @bind:culture="culture" />
<input @bind="date" @bind:format="yyyy-MM-dd" />
<input @bind:get="name" @bind:set="SetNameAsync" />
<input @bind="searchText" @bind:after="SearchAsync" />
```

Supported culture and format choices retain their existing meaning. Asynchronous setters and after-callbacks retain their supported completion, ordering, and error behavior.

For a decimal amount, the relevant lowering is:

```csharp
var attributeValue = BindConverter.FormatValue(amount, culture);
var callback = EventCallback.Factory.CreateBinder(
    this, __value => amount = __value, amount, culture);
```

For the asynchronous name setter, the factory receives the asynchronous setter rather than a replacement assignment:

```csharp
var callback = EventCallback.Factory.CreateBinder(
    this, SetNameAsync, name);
```

Supported format values reach both applicable formatting and parsing operations. After-callbacks retain their existing compiler-generated setter/callback composition.

### Use well-known framework conversion

The framework provides reusable conversion for a bounded default inventory rather than generating one implementation per binding:

| Category | Default coverage |
|---|---|
| Text | string |
| Boolean | bool and bool?, preserving conditional-attribute versus select-text behavior |
| Numeric direct paths | short, int, long, float, double, decimal, and their nullable versions |
| Date/time | DateTime, DateTimeOffset, DateOnly, TimeOnly, and their nullable versions |
| Identifier | Guid and Guid?, preserving supported parsing/formatting |
| Common arrays | Supported one-dimensional arrays of the common scalar types, including nullable value-type elements and string[] |
| Enums | Shared trim/AOT-compatible Enum operations, including Type-based operations for unconstrained generic callers and nullable enums |

This list reflects existing direct conversion cases rather than assuming every C# primitive already has a dedicated path. Additional primitive types such as byte, sbyte, ushort, uint, ulong, and char require coverage review against their existing converter behavior before inclusion; their existing supported behavior must not be lost.

Common nullable and one-dimensional array combinations can use a static table of closed implementations. Reference nullability does not require separate runtime conversion instances. Supported one-dimensional arrays of enum or custom-convertible elements need statically available element conversion rather than runtime MakeGenericMethod/MakeGenericType.

For a statically known enum, shared conversion can use Enum.TryParse<TEnum> and Enum.IsDefined<TEnum>. Unconstrained generic code can use the existing Type-based enum operations instead of closing a constrained generic method through reflection. Parsing retains current case sensitivity, empty-input behavior, and rejection of undefined enum values, including unnamed flags combinations.

For example:

```razor
<select @bind="customer.Status">
    <option value="Active">Active</option>
    <option value="Inactive">Inactive</option>
</select>
<select @bind="selectedStatuses" multiple>
    <option value="Active">Active</option>
    <option value="Inactive">Inactive</option>
</select>
```

Here Status is an OrderStatus enum and selectedStatuses is an OrderStatus array. These native element bindings let Razor see the concrete conversion types directly, unlike conversion inside a generic input component. The single-selection lowering has this shape:

```csharp
builder.OpenElement(0, "select");
builder.AddAttribute(1, "value", BindConverter.FormatValue(customer.Status));
builder.AddAttribute(2, "onchange",
    EventCallback.Factory.CreateBinder<OrderStatus>(
        this, __value => customer.Status = __value, customer.Status));
builder.SetUpdatesAttributeName("value");
// Option content is omitted.
builder.CloseElement();
```

For multiple selection, the event carries a string array. Conversion allocates a target OrderStatus array and converts each selected string using the shared enum conversion. Razor can statically establish both the target array and its element conversion; it must not cause runtime reflected generic construction.

The existing BindConverter array implementation creates its element-parser factory through MakeGenericMethod/Invoke. This feature replaces that discovery/construction while preserving element order, empty-array results, failure behavior, and supported formatting. Concrete-array static APIs and generic-array converter delivery remain integration questions, not evidence that arrays already satisfy strict execution.

### Bind a statically known custom type

A custom type associates its converter using System.ComponentModel.TypeConverterAttribute:

```csharp
[TypeConverter(typeof(MoneyConverter))]
public readonly record struct Money(decimal Amount);
```

MoneyConverter implements supported string conversion through TypeConverter. Razor can inspect the attribute's typeof argument as a type symbol and reference the converter directly:

```razor
<input @bind="invoice.Total" />
```

For a supported accessible parameterless constructor, the generated component can retain a converter field:

```csharp
private readonly TypeConverter __moneyConverter = new MoneyConverter();
```

The corresponding proposed lowering supplies that converter to both directions:

```csharp
builder.OpenElement(0, "input");
builder.AddAttribute(1, "value",
    BindConverter.FormatValue(
        invoice.Total, converter: __moneyConverter,
        culture: null, format: null));
builder.AddAttribute(2, "onchange",
    EventCallback.Factory.CreateBinder<Money>(
        this, __value => invoice.Total = __value, invoice.Total,
        converter: __moneyConverter, culture: null, format: null));
builder.SetUpdatesAttributeName("value");
builder.CloseElement();
```

No TypeDescriptor.GetConverter call, generated converter class, generic binder interface, or cascading request is needed at this known-type binding site. The field illustrates reuse outside the render method, not a finalized lifetime/caching policy.

Converter-backed formatting and parsing preserve applicable direction, culture, failure, and null/empty behavior. TypeConverter does not itself define the complete binding format contract; the framework must preserve existing format support without promising that arbitrary converters accept format strings.

### Supply a custom converter to generic code

A non-generic TypeConverter cannot by itself identify which generic target type a cascading request serves. A typed carrier supplies that association without implementing conversion:

```csharp
public sealed class TypeConverterAttributeBinder<T>
{
    public TypeConverterAttributeBinder(TypeConverter value)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(value);
        Value = value;
    }

    public TypeConverter Value { get; }
}
```

T identifies the target type for lookup and cascading matching. Value returns the converter; the class has no parsing or formatting methods. Direct generated construction does not require a preservation annotation on T because the carrier does not discover its members.

A generic component can originate a binding to local state:

```razor
@typeparam TValue

<input @bind="localValue" />

@code {
    [CascadingParameter]
    internal TypeConverterAttributeBinder<TValue>? AttributeConverter { get; set; }

    private TValue localValue = default!;
}
```

An application uses the closed component without supplying a bound value:

```razor
<GenericEditor TValue="Money" />
```

Framework conversion handles common types and enums directly. When TValue needs custom conversion, a fixed cascading source supplies TypeConverterAttributeBinder<Money>, constructed from the already-known MoneyConverter. Components do not receive a resolver and do not call TypeDescriptor to discover converters.

Razor recognizes the matching accessible cascading property and uses its Value when supplied. Proposed generic lowering is:

```csharp
var converter = AttributeConverter?.Value;

builder.OpenElement(0, "input");
builder.AddAttribute(1, "value",
    BindConverter.FormatValue(
        localValue, converter: converter, culture: null, format: null));
builder.AddAttribute(2, "onchange",
    EventCallback.Factory.CreateBinder<TValue>(
        this, __value => localValue = __value, localValue,
        converter: converter, culture: null, format: null));
builder.SetUpdatesAttributeName("value");
builder.CloseElement();
```

In this proposed overload shape, an absent converter permits only framework-supported conversion. If custom conversion is required and not supplied, strict execution reports missing support rather than switching to TypeDescriptor discovery. The nullable property allows framework-supported generic cases to avoid an unnecessary custom-converter source; exact overload and compiler-selection rules remain open.

Fixedness belongs to the supplier, not CascadingParameterAttribute. The supplied carrier/converter reference stays stable for the source's lifetime, avoiding recipient change subscriptions; culture and format remain per-operation arguments. A stable reference does not prove that the converter is stateless or thread-safe.

Closed carrier instances or factories can be recorded in the selected application's definitions and supplied through CascadingValue or equivalent framework integration. Dictionary lookup and cascading matching retain the target type identity; supplying the wrong converter remains a runtime contract error because TypeConverter returns object rather than T.

### Integrate framework and custom input components

Generic inputs need conversion even when their parent only forwards typed values:

```razor
@typeparam TValue

<InputSelect TValue="TValue" @bind-Value="localValue" />

@code {
    private TValue localValue = default!;
}
```

The relevant wrapper lowering remains:

```csharp
builder.OpenComponent<InputSelect<TValue>>(0);
builder.AddComponentParameter(1, "Value", localValue);
builder.AddComponentParameter(2, "ValueChanged",
    EventCallback.Factory.Create<TValue>(
        this, __value => localValue = __value));
// Other existing component parameters are omitted.
builder.CloseComponent();
```

InputSelect<TValue> performs conversion internally. If its TValue needs a custom converter, the input declares its own typed cascading carrier property; the wrapper does not forward the converter as an ordinary parameter. The same mechanism is available to custom inputs:

```csharp
[CascadingParameter]
internal TypeConverterAttributeBinder<TValue>? AttributeConverter { get; set; }
```

A component that only forwards Value and ValueChanged needs no converter merely because it is generic. An input that performs conversion uses the supplied converter with the framework conversion APIs, preserving its local state, validation messages, and notifications. Existing InputBase formatting/parsing overrides remain supported; their detailed interaction with supplied converters needs a defined policy.

InputSelect<TValue> selects its multiple-selection path when TValue is an array. It receives a string array from the element callback, then calls BindConverter to convert the elements to the target array type. For custom-convertible array elements, the required converter belongs to the element type, not necessarily the array type; generic discovery of that element requirement and statically available array conversion must be designed explicitly. Single-select formatting currently defaults to InputBase's ToString-based behavior, with InputSelect Boolean specialization; supplying a converter must not silently replace that with converter-based formatting.

### Diagnose unsupported conversion and preserve ordinary invalid input

Invalid element input retains the existing conversion-failure and empty-input setter behavior. InputBase-derived inputs retain rejected text, parsing validation messages, local value updates, and field/validation notifications rather than writing invalid values to the model.

A missing custom converter, unsupported constructor/association, or converter result of the wrong type is a support/configuration error, not ordinary invalid user input. Statically knowable missing/unsupported requirements produce actionable build diagnostics naming the affected type/member/binding and corrective action. Runtime-only support failures report explicitly instead of falling back to reflection or appearing successful; they must not be swallowed as an ordinary parse failure.

Statically visible TypeConverterAttribute(typeof(...)) associations are the baseline. String-named attributes, inherited associations, and runtime TypeDescriptor registration/providers require explicit support rules. Directly constructing a converter removes discovery, but its implementation must itself be trim/AOT-compatible; preservation annotations cannot guarantee that or make runtime code generation available.

### Upgrade without enabling additional AOT features

Existing applications retain their binding syntax, supported converters, and custom inputs without mandatory new AOT-related declarations or configuration. Upgrading alone introduces no new build/publish warnings. Strict diagnostics and generated-support requirements apply when additional AOT features or checks are enabled.

Issues.Title: Blazor Web Worker template imports JavaScript initializers into the worker
Issues.Body:
# Blazor Web Worker template imports JavaScript initializers into the worker

## Description

The .NET 11 Blazor Web Worker template reuses the client app's boot configuration and imports its library JavaScript initializers into the worker, including initializers from libraries that the worker project does not reference.

This is a general initializer-isolation issue, not specific to a component library: any library initializer, or one of its imported dependencies, that assumes a page environment can fail when loaded in a worker. Initializers that access `document`, for example, encounter `ReferenceError: document is not defined`. Worker-compatible initializers may run successfully, but are still inherited from the client app rather than isolated by the worker's project references.

**Ignite UI Blazor Lite is a real-world example.** Its initializer imports DOM-dependent Lit code. In the linked repro, Ignite UI is referenced only by the client project; **the worker project does not reference Ignite UI**, and its generated template files are unchanged.

## Reproduction

[Repro project: danroth27/BlazorWebWorkerIgniteUIRepro](https://github.com/danroth27/BlazorWebWorkerIgniteUIRepro)

Run the client using the command in the README and open the browser console. The page renders an Ignite UI Combo Box and automatically starts the worker to call its generated `Greet` method.

The repro has only the standalone client and generated worker projects. It does not use Aspire, Syncfusion, or a custom JavaScript initializer.

## Actual behavior

The worker imports library initializers from the client app regardless of whether the worker project references those libraries. In the Ignite UI example, the Combo Box initializes successfully in the page, but the worker also requests:

```text
_content/IgniteUI.Blazor/IgniteUI.Blazor.Lite.<fingerprint>.lib.module.js
_content/IgniteUI.Blazor/app.BFhi3J2R.bundle.js
_content/IgniteUI.Blazor/igniteui-core.cH5HOuKB.bundle.js
_content/IgniteUI.Blazor/lit-html.js
_content/IgniteUI.Blazor/api.js
_content/IgniteUI.Blazor/interop.js
```

The DOM-dependent import fails in `lit-html.js`, and the runtime logs:

```text
MONO_WASM: Failed to import library initializer '[object Object]': ReferenceError: document is not defined
```

The worker still returns `Hello, World!`. The runtime catches and logs this initializer import failure; this repro does **not** demonstrate a worker startup crash. The underlying JavaScript exception also interrupted debugging in the app where I encountered the issue.

## Expected behavior

There should be a supported, discoverable way to control which library JavaScript initializers run in a worker, so that starting a worker does not require every library used by the client app to support the worker environment.

In particular, a computation-only worker should be able to reuse the app's .NET assets without importing page-only library initializers and their dependencies.

Worker-safe runtime initializers may still be necessary. This is not a request to indiscriminately disable every initializer in every worker.

## Investigation

The generated worker imports the client's `dotnet.js` and starts another runtime with the same boot configuration, including its library initializer lists. In the linked example, the Ignite UI initializer is included in `resources.modulesAfterRuntimeReady`:

```javascript
const { dotnet } = await import(dotnetJsUrl);
const { getAssemblyExports, getConfig } = await dotnet.create();
```

Selecting the worker assembly with `getAssemblyExports` happens after startup and does not isolate the runtime from the client's library initializers.

For a computation-only worker, I worked around this in the original app by clearing the ready-phase initializer list in `onConfigLoaded` before `dotnet.create()` completes:

```javascript
const { getAssemblyExports, getConfig } = await dotnet
    .withModuleConfig({
        onConfigLoaded(config) {
            config.resources.modulesAfterRuntimeReady = [];
        }
    })
    .create();
```

This prevents the Ignite UI/Lit imports in that worker. **The linked repro deliberately does not include this workaround.** Clearing the entire list may remove worker-compatible initializers too, and this hook does not address imports in earlier initializer phases.

## Environment

- .NET SDK: `11.0.100`
- Target framework: `net11.0`
- Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly: `11.0.0`
- IgniteUI.Blazor.Lite: `1.0.1`
- Windows, Microsoft Edge
- Worker generated with `dotnet new blazorwebworker`

Issues.Title: Kestrel HTTP/3: a peer reset of a not-yet-identified bidirectional stream faults the whole connection
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

If a client resets a bidirectional stream (RESET_STREAM) before Kestrel has read the stream's type header, Kestrel faults and closes the whole HTTP/3 connection. Every request and WebTransport session on that connection ends.

In `Http3Connection.ProcessRequestsAsync`, the accept loop reads each new stream's header inline:

- `pendingStream.ReadNextStreamHeaderAsync(...)`
- `CreateAndAddWebTransportStream` → `ReadNextStreamHeaderAsync` (the WebTransport session id)

The per-stream `try` only catches `Http3PendingStreamException`. When the peer resets the stream, the read throws `ConnectionResetException` ("Stream aborted by peer (0)"). That exception skips the per-stream handler and reaches the connection-level `catch (ConnectionResetException)`, which ends the connection. Kestrel then sends GOAWAY and aborts the connection with error 256, "The HTTP/3 connection faulted."

WebTransport clients hit this all the time. A browser or native client that opens a stream and cancels it straight away resets a stream whose header Kestrel may not have read yet. Under load that brings down the whole session, even though only one stream was cancelled.

### Expected Behavior

A reset of a stream that hasn't been identified yet aborts only that stream: it is logged as an unidentified-stream abort, like `Http3PendingStreamException`. The connection and the other streams carry on.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run Kestrel with HTTP/3 and WebTransport enabled (`IHttpWebTransportFeature.AcceptAsync`, then loop on `AcceptStreamAsync`).
2. From a QUIC WebTransport client on one session, open a bidirectional stream, write the WebTransport stream header (`0x41`, session id), then reset the stream at once. Repeat this in a loop. We used quinn: `open_bi`, `write_all(header)`, `reset(0)`.
3. Usually within tens of streams, the session is closed by the server with 256. The server's debug log shows:

```
dbug: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel.Http3[53]  Connection id "…": GOAWAY stream ID 4.
dbug: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel.Http3[45]  Trace id "…:00000002": HTTP/3 stream error "H3_NO_ERROR". An abort is being sent to the stream.
      Microsoft.AspNetCore.Connections.ConnectionAbortedException: The HTTP/3 connection faulted.
      Connection id "…" aborted by application with error code 256 because: "The HTTP/3 connection faulted.".
```

Ending the stream with FIN instead of RESET_STREAM avoids it: 120 open/close cycles on one session complete.

### Exceptions (if any)

`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Connections.ConnectionResetException: Stream aborted by peer (0). ---> System.Net.Quic.QuicException: Stream aborted by peer (0).`

### .NET Version

11.0.100 (Linux x64, libmsquic 2.5)

### Anything else?

Related to the TODO in the same code ("needs to get dispatched off of the accept loop", #42789), and to the WebTransport issues we filed earlier: #70384, #70386 and #70395.

Issues.Title: Kestrel WebTransport never releases finished streams: session stalls after 100 streams and leaks ~3.7 KB per stream
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

On a WebTransport session, Kestrel never releases a finished stream, so streams pile up for the whole session. This causes two problems:

1. **The session stalls after 100 streams.** The per-stream `QuicStreamContext` is never disposed, so msquic never gives the peer more bidirectional stream credit. Once `MaxBidirectionalStreamCount` (100 by default) streams have been used, the client's next `OpenBidirectionalStream` waits forever, even though every earlier stream finished long ago.
2. **The session leaks about 3.7 KB per stream** until it ends. Each `WebTransportStream` stays in `WebTransportSession._openStreams`, along with its `QuicStreamContext`, pipes and abort `ExceptionDispatchInfo`.

The cause, in `src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/Internal/WebTransport/WebTransportStream.cs`:

- The constructor registers on `context.StreamContext.ConnectionClosed` to call `WebTransportSession.TryRemoveStream`. That registration is the only path that removes the stream from `_openStreams`.
- `WebTransportStream.DisposeAsync()` first disposes `_connectionClosedRegistration`, then completes the duplex pipe. The app disposes the `ConnectionContext` it got from `AcceptStreamAsync` when it is done, so that removal callback never runs.
- Nothing disposes the underlying stream context (`Http3StreamContext.StreamContext`, the `QuicStreamContext`). In `Http3Connection.CreateAndAddWebTransportStream`, ownership passes to the `WebTransportStream`, and that type never disposes it. Request streams are different: their stream lifetime handler disposes the context.

### Expected Behavior

Disposing a stream from `IWebTransportSession.AcceptStreamAsync` (or finishing it) removes it from the session, disposes its stream context, and returns the QUIC stream credit. A session should then serve any number of sequential streams with flat memory.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Start a Kestrel HTTP/3 server with WebTransport enabled. For each accepted stream, read one message, write a reply, then `await stream.DisposeAsync()`:

```csharp
app.Run(async ctx =>
{
    var session = await ctx.Features.GetRequiredFeature<IHttpWebTransportFeature>().AcceptAsync(ctx.RequestAborted);
    while (await session.AcceptStreamAsync(ctx.RequestAborted) is { } stream)
    {
        _ = Task.Run(async () =>
        {
            await using (stream)
            {
                var read = await stream.Transport.Input.ReadAsync();
                await stream.Transport.Output.WriteAsync(read.Buffer.ToArray());
                stream.Transport.Input.AdvanceTo(read.Buffer.End);
                await stream.Transport.Output.CompleteAsync();
            }
        });
    }
});
```

2. From any WebTransport client (we used a .NET `QuicConnection` client and a Rust quinn client), open bidirectional streams one at a time on a single session. Each stream should send a message, read the reply to FIN, and close.

Results:

- **Stream 101 never opens.** Here is a server debug log for one stream: the stream is accepted, writes shut down gracefully, and nothing else happens. msquic sends no new MAX_STREAMS.
- **Heap growth, measured in-process with `GC.GetTotalMemory(true)` after each round:**

| After calls | Managed heap |
| --- | --- |
| 10,000 | 46 MB |
| 20,000 | 84 MB |
| 30,000 | 121 MB |
| 40,000 | 158 MB |

  To get past the stall for this measurement, our test disposed the stream context as in the workaround below.
- **`dumpheap -stat` after 20k calls:** 22,000 × `ConcurrentDictionary<long, WebTransportStream>+Node`, 22,000 × `WebTransportStream`, 22,003 × `QuicStreamContext`, 21,998 × `ExceptionDispatchInfo`.

**Workaround.** After the app is done with a stream:

1. Call the internal `WebTransportSession.TryRemoveStream(streamId)` through `[UnsafeAccessor]` with `[UnsafeAccessorType(...WebTransportSession...)]`. It also disposes the `WebTransportStream`.
2. Then dispose `stream.Features`, which is the `QuicStreamContext`.

With both steps, 40,000 calls on one session stay flat at about 1.7 MB, and the session runs without a limit.

### Exceptions (if any)

None. The client just waits for stream credit forever.

### .NET Version

11.0.100 (Linux x64, libmsquic 2.5)

### Anything else?

Related WebTransport issues we filed: #70384 (draft H3_DATAGRAM codepoint) and #70386 (client uni-stream reader completed at FIN).
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "Kestrel WebTransport never releases finished streams: session stalls after 100 streams and leaks ~3.7 KB per stream" (#70395)

Issues.Title: Blazor Hybrid Windows publish still copies precompressed .gz and .br assets from referenced RCLs into publish/wwwroot
Issues.Body:
### Description

Blazor Hybrid sets `<CompressionEnabled>false</CompressionEnabled>` (via `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebView`'s `StaticWebAssets.Groups.targets`) because `WebViewManager` serves static assets locally without HTTP content-encoding negotiation. However, when a Blazor Hybrid app references a Razor class library (`ProjectReference`), the RCL still builds with `CompressionEnabled=true` by default and contributes precompressed `.gz` and `.br` (`AssetRole="Alternative"`) static web assets to the consuming app's publish manifest.

While https://github.com/dotnet/maui/pull/33917 (for https://github.com/dotnet/maui/issues/33773) filtered `AssetRole='Alternative'` `.gz`/`.br` items out of `@(MauiAsset)` in `ConvertStaticWebAssetsToMauiAssets` (fixing Android APKs), it did not remove them from `@(StaticWebAsset)` / `_PublishStaticWebAssetsPreserveNewest`. As a result, publishing a Blazor Hybrid app on Windows (MAUI Windows, WPF, or WinForms) still runs `GeneratePublishCompressedStaticWebAssets` (Brotli) for the RCL and copies redundant `.gz` and `.br` files for every RCL asset into `publish/wwwroot/_content/<Rcl>/`.

Discovered during validation testing in https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/68814#issuecomment-5536899858.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a new MAUI Blazor Hybrid app and a Razor Class Library from templates and reference the RCL:
   ```powershell
   dotnet new maui-blazor -n MauiHybridApp
   dotnet new razorclasslib -n MyRcl
   dotnet add MauiHybridApp/MauiHybridApp.csproj reference MyRcl/MyRcl.csproj
   ```
2. Publish the MAUI app for Windows:
   ```powershell
   dotnet publish MauiHybridApp/MauiHybridApp.csproj -c Release -f net11.0-windows10.0.19041.0
   ```
3. Inspect `MauiHybridApp/bin/Release/net11.0-windows10.0.19041.0/win-x64/publish/wwwroot/_content/MyRcl/`.
4. **Expected:** Only uncompressed RCL assets (`exampleJsInterop.js`, `MyRcl.<hash>.bundle.scp.css`, `background.png`) are published when `CompressionEnabled=false`.
5. **Actual:** Precompressed `.gz` and `.br` files (`exampleJsInterop.js.gz`, `exampleJsInterop.js.br`, `MyRcl.<hash>.bundle.scp.css.gz`, `MyRcl.<hash>.bundle.scp.css.br`) are also copied into `publish/wwwroot/_content/MyRcl/`.

Issues.Title: Renderer.Dispose does not clear _eventBindings or cascading parameter subscriptions, retaining disposed components
Issues.Body:
### Description

When `Renderer.Dispose(bool disposing)` tears down a renderer, it clears `_componentStateById` and `_componentStateByComponent`, but:
1. It never clears `_eventBindings` or `_eventHandlerIdReplacements` (`Renderer.cs`). Any component that rendered a DOM event handler (e.g., `@onclick`) remains referenced by its `EventCallback` delegate in `_eventBindings`.
2. It calls `ComponentState.DisposeAsync()` rather than `DisposeInBatchAsync()`, skipping `RemoveCascadingParameterSubscriptions()`, which leaves disposed `ComponentState` instances subscribed to longer-lived `CascadingValueSource<T>` suppliers (e.g., root/singleton cascading values).
3. `WebViewManager.DisposeAsyncCore()` awaits `_currentPageContext.DisposeAsync()` without setting `_currentPageContext = null`.

If the disposed `Renderer` or `WebViewManager` remains reachable (or while subscribed to a singleton `CascadingValueSource`), all components with DOM event handlers and their fields (such as `IJSObjectReference` modules) stay pinned in memory.

Discovered during validation testing in https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/68813#issuecomment-5583915474 (Finding 1).

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Render a component with an `@onclick` handler inside a `WebViewManager` / `Renderer` (such as `SlowCall.razor` in https://github.com/surya3655/blazor-hybrid-teardown-validation).
2. Dispose the `WebViewManager` / `Renderer` while keeping a reference to the disposed manager/renderer (or subscribe the component to a singleton `CascadingValueSource<T>`).
3. Force GC (`GC.Collect(); GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers(); GC.Collect();`).

5. **Actual:** Components with `@onclick` (and their `IJSObjectReference` fields) remain rooted via `Renderer._eventBindings`.

Issues.Title: WebViewJSRuntime / JSRuntime never cancels or faults in-flight _pendingTasks when disconnected
Issues.Body:
### Description

When `PageContext.DisposeAsync()` calls `WebViewJSRuntime.MarkAsDisconnected()` (added in #66259), only *subsequent* `BeginInvokeJS` calls throw `JSDisconnectedException`. Calls that were already in flight in `JSRuntime._pendingTasks` are never faulted or canceled. Because `WebViewJSRuntime` has `DefaultAsyncTimeout = null`, any in-flight `InvokeAsync` call without a `CancellationToken` remains pending in `_pendingTasks` forever, pinning its continuation and any `async` state machine awaiting it. (Similarly, `RemoteJSRuntime.MarkPermanentlyDisconnected()` leaves in-flight tasks pending until `JSInteropDefaultCallTimeout` expires or indefinitely if passed a non-canceling token.)

Discovered during validation testing in https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/68813#issuecomment-5583915474 (Finding 1).

### Steps to Reproduce

1. In a Blazor Hybrid component, start a long-running JS interop call without a `CancellationToken` (e.g., `var task = module.InvokeAsync<string>("slowCall", 15_000).AsTask();` as in `SlowCall.razor` from https://github.com/surya3655/blazor-hybrid-teardown-validation).
2. Tear down the `BlazorWebView` or reload the page while the call is still in flight.
3. Observe `task.Status` after teardown.
4. **Expected:** In-flight tasks in `_pendingTasks` transition to a faulted (`JSDisconnectedException`) or canceled state when the runtime disconnects.
5. **Actual:** `task` stays `WaitingForActivation` indefinitely; continuations and awaiting state machines never complete.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "WebViewJSRuntime / JSRuntime never cancels or faults in-flight _pendingTasks when disconnected" (#70392)

Issues.Title: [Blazor] Interactive server component added while the circuit's first UpdateRootComponents is still pending is never rendered ("Cannot update existing state: previous state has not been cleared")
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Describe the bug In a Blazor Web App with interactive server islands, an `UpdateRootComponents` call that arrives while the circuit's **first** `UpdateRootComponents` is still waiting for quiescence fails its persistent-state restore, and the root components it adds are never rendered. The page stays a non-interactive prerender until the next navigation. Nothing is logged: `CircuitHost` logs "Update root components succeeded", no error reaches the browser, and the exception is only visible as an unobserved task exception. How it happens on `main` ([`31ca3ac`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/tree/31ca3acb381c94cef86ce9af46292efbda31f273)), identical on `release/10.0`: 1. The first update restores the store with `InitialValue` and sets `shouldWaitForQuiescence`; the store is cleared only in its `finally`, after every added component has finished its first render ([CircuitHost.cs#L802-L823](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/31ca3acb381c94cef86ce9af46292efbda31f273/src/Components/Server/src/Circuits/CircuitHost.cs#L802-L823), [#L857-L865](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/31ca3acb381c94cef86ce9af46292efbda31f273/src/Components/Server/src/Circuits/CircuitHost.cs#L857-L865)). Keys that no component takes stay in `PersistentComponentState._existingState` until then. Here that is page B's `[PersistentState]` value: the first batch always carries the state read from the document when the server boot started ([Boot.Server.Common.ts#L47](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/31ca3acb381c94cef86ce9af46292efbda31f273/src/Components/Web.JS/src/Boot.Server.Common.ts#L47), [CircuitManager.ts#L98-L104](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/31ca3acb381c94cef86ce9af46292efbda31f273/src/Components/Web.JS/src/Platform/Circuits/CircuitManager.ts#L98-L104)), which is page B's, while the component it adds is page A's island. 2. `ComponentHub.UpdateRootComponents` does not await the circuit ([ComponentHub.cs#L237](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/31ca3acb381c94cef86ce9af46292efbda31f273/src/Components/Server/src/ComponentHub.cs#L237)), so a second batch (the Back navigation) runs on the dispatcher while the first one awaits quiescence. It gets `RestoreContext.ValueUpdate` and an `EnqueueRestore` task ([CircuitHost.cs#L808-L812](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/31ca3acb381c94cef86ce9af46292efbda31f273/src/Components/Server/src/Circuits/CircuitHost.cs#L808-L812), [#L870-L878](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/31ca3acb381c94cef86ce9af46292efbda31f273/src/Components/Server/src/Circuits/CircuitHost.cs#L870-L878)). 3. That restore calls `PersistentComponentState.UpdateExistingState`, which throws because the first batch's keys are still there ([PersistentComponentState.cs#L247-L250](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/31ca3acb381c94cef86ce9af46292efbda31f273/src/Components/Components/src/PersistentComponentState.cs#L247-L250), called from [ComponentStatePersistenceManager.cs#L80](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/31ca3acb381c94cef86ce9af46292efbda31f273/src/Components/Components/src/PersistentState/ComponentStatePersistenceManager.cs#L80)). 4. `WebRootComponentManager.AddRootComponentAsync` has already added the component to the renderer, then awaits that faulted task and never calls `RenderAsync` ([WebRootComponentManager.cs#L54-L57](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/31ca3acb381c94cef86ce9af46292efbda31f273/src/Components/Shared/src/WebRootComponentManager.cs#L54-L57)). 5. For any batch but the first, `pendingTasks` is `null`, so the add task is not observed ([CircuitHost.cs#L888-L890](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/31ca3acb381c94cef86ce9af46292efbda31f273/src/Components/Server/src/Circuits/CircuitHost.cs#L888-L890), [#L902-L908](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/31ca3acb381c94cef86ce9af46292efbda31f273/src/Components/Server/src/Circuits/CircuitHost.cs#L902-L908), [#L927-L930](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/31ca3acb381c94cef86ce9af46292efbda31f273/src/Components/Server/src/Circuits/CircuitHost.cs#L927-L930)). The batch reports success and `JS.EndUpdateRootComponents` is sent. In a real app the window is short but easy to hit: a reader presses a link in the moment before the page goes live, the next page's island does a slow read, and they go Back. ### Expected Behavior The component added by the later batch becomes interactive, as it does when the same navigation happens after the circuit is up. If its state cannot be restored, the failure is at least logged / reported like other `UpdateRootComponents` failures, rather than leaving a dead prerender with a "succeeded" log. ### Actual Behavior Page B's island stays a static prerender (no event handlers, no re-render) until the next navigation. The server logs only "Update root components succeeded"; the `InvalidOperationException` below surfaces solely through `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException`. ### Steps To Reproduce `dotnet new blazor -o BlazorRace --interactivity Server --all-interactive false`, then add these files (the two `Program.cs` lines only make the swallowed exception visible; we also dropped `app.UseHttpsRedirection()` to run on plain HTTP, which does not matter). `Components/Pages/ListPage.razor` (page B) ```razor @page "/list"

Page B

Go to page A ``` `Components/ItemList.razor` ```razor

@(RendererInfo.IsInteractive ? "interactive" : "static")

    @foreach (var item in Items ?? []) {
  • @item
    • }
@code { [PersistentState] public string[]? Items { get; set; } protected override void OnInitialized() { Items ??= ["one", "two", "three"]; } } ``` `Components/Pages/SlowPage.razor` (page A) ```razor @page "/slow"

Page A

Go to page B ``` `Components/SlowPanel.razor` ```razor

@status

@code { private string status = "static"; protected override async Task OnParametersSetAsync() { if (RendererInfo.IsInteractive) { status = "loading"; await Task.Delay(3000); // stands in for a slow read status = "interactive"; } } } ``` `Program.cs`, after `var app = builder.Build();` ```csharp TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException += (_, e) => app.Logger.LogError(e.Exception, "Unobserved task exception"); _ = Task.Run(async () => { while (true) { await Task.Delay(500); GC.Collect(); GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers(); } }); ``` Steps: 1. Open `/list` and press "Go to page A" before the circuit has started (throttling the network in DevTools makes this easy). 2. On page A, while it shows "loading", press the browser's Back button. 3. Page B is shown, but "static" never changes to "interactive". The server logs the exception below (twice: the restore task and the add task). Navigating again recovers. Scripted with Playwright (`playwright-core` 1.59.1, Chromium), `/_blazor/negotiate` delayed 1 s so the link is always pressed before the circuit starts, then Back as soon as page A shows "loading": | | .NET 10.0.11 | .NET 10.0.14 | |---|---|---| | link pressed before the circuit starts | 20/20 runs: page B never interactive | 20/20 | | same, no artificial delay (the click only sometimes beats the circuit) | 2/10 | 0/20 | | control: link pressed after page B is interactive | 0/20 | 0/20 |
Playwright script ```js import { chromium } from 'playwright-core'; const base = 'http://127.0.0.1:5311'; const browser = await chromium.launch(); const page = await (await browser.newContext()).newPage(); await page.route('**/_blazor/negotiate**', async r => { await new Promise(x => setTimeout(x, 1000)); await r.continue(); }); await page.goto(`${base}/list`, { waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded' }); await page.click('#to-slow'); // before the circuit is up await page.locator('h1', { hasText: 'Page A' }).waitFor(); await page.locator('#slow-status', { hasText: 'loading' }).waitFor(); // first batch still waiting for quiescence await page.evaluate(() => history.back()); await page.locator('h1', { hasText: 'Page B' }).waitFor(); await page.locator('#list-status', { hasText: 'interactive' }).waitFor({ timeout: 10000 }); // times out await browser.close(); ```
### Exceptions (if any) ``` fail: BlazorRace[0] Unobserved task exception System.AggregateException: A Task's exception(s) were not observed either by Waiting on the Task or accessing its Exception property. As a result, the unobserved exception was rethrown by the finalizer thread. (Cannot update existing state: previous state has not been cleared or state is not initialized.) ---> System.InvalidOperationException: Cannot update existing state: previous state has not been cleared or state is not initialized. at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.PersistentComponentState.UpdateExistingState(IDictionary`2 state, RestoreContext context) at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Infrastructure.ComponentStatePersistenceManager.RestoreStateAsync(IPersistentComponentStateStore store, RestoreContext context) at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Server.Circuits.CircuitHost.EnqueueRestore(TaskCompletionSource taskCompletionSource, ComponentStatePersistenceManager manager, RestoreContext context, IPersistentComponentStateStore store) at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Server.Circuits.RemoteRenderer.WebRootComponentManager.AddRootComponentAsync(Int32 ssrComponentId, Type componentType, Nullable`1 key, WebRootComponentParameters parameters) --- End of inner exception stack trace --- dbug: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Server.Circuits.CircuitHost[112] Update root components succeeded. ``` ### .NET Version 10.0.14 (SDK 10.0.403); also 10.0.11 (SDK 10.0.400) ### Anything else? - ASP.NET Core 10.0.14+0427b9abbead3fa64c6655eb4290c537397131fa, Ubuntu 24.04 x64, Chromium 147 (Playwright 1.59.1). Not tried on a 11.0 preview; the code in the links above is unchanged on `main`. - #67980 / #68891 fixed the same kind of silently discarded activation task for WebAssembly. On Server, the add task is observed only for the circuit's first batch. - With `ItemList` keeping its items in a plain field instead of `[PersistentState]` (nothing left untaken in the first batch's store), the same script passes: 0/10 on 10.0.14. - Related: #70391 (a second Server bug in the same window: a navigation made before the renderer attaches never reaches the circuit).

Issues.Title: Kestrel WebTransport completes a client unidirectional stream's reader at FIN, before the app reads buffered data
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

When a WebTransport client opens a **unidirectional** stream, writes some bytes and finishes it (FIN), Kestrel can complete the application's `PipeReader` for that stream before the app has read the buffered data. The app then gets:

```
System.InvalidOperationException: Reading is not allowed after reader was completed.
```

Or it reads a truncated stream. This happens intermittently: about 2 in 8 runs on loopback with no proxy in between.

From reading `main`, the path looks like this:

1. `WebTransportStream`'s constructor registers on `context.StreamContext.ConnectionClosed`, and the callback calls `WebTransportSession.TryRemoveStream(streamId)`. The comment there says it "will not trigger if closed only of of the directions of a stream. Stream must be fully ended before this will be called."
2. An inbound unidirectional stream has only one direction, so it counts as "fully ended" as soon as the peer's FIN is received by the transport, even while that data still sits unread in the pipe.
3. `TryRemoveStream` calls `stream.DisposeAsync().AsTask().GetAwaiter().GetResult()`.
4. `WebTransportStream.DisposeAsync` runs `await _duplexPipe.Input.CompleteAsync()`. That completes the **application's** reader while the application may still be reading it.

Bidirectional streams don't hit this in practice, because the application's side stays open until it writes and completes.

Files:
- `src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/Internal/WebTransport/WebTransportStream.cs` (the `ConnectionClosed` registration and `DisposeAsync`)
- `src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/Internal/WebTransport/WebTransportSession.cs` (`TryRemoveStream`)

### Expected Behavior

Data a peer sent before its FIN on a unidirectional stream can always be read in full by the application. The stream should be cleaned up only after the application has completed its reader, or disposed the stream itself, rather than when the transport sees the stream end.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Linux, libmsquic 2.6.2, .NET SDK `11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148`. A Kestrel app with `WebTransportAndH3Datagrams` enabled, `UseQuic()`, and `Http1AndHttp2AndHttp3` on loopback.
2. Handler:

   ```csharp
   app.Run(async context =>
   {
       var session = await context.Features.GetRequiredFeature<IHttpWebTransportFeature>()
           .AcceptAsync(context.RequestAborted);
       var stream = await session.AcceptStreamAsync(context.RequestAborted);
       await using (stream!)
       {
           using var buffer = new MemoryStream();
           await stream!.Transport.Input.CopyToAsync(buffer, context.RequestAborted); // throws intermittently
           Console.WriteLine(buffer.Length);
       }
   });
   ```

3. Client (any WebTransport client): open a session, open a unidirectional stream (type `0x54` + session id), write 4 bytes, finish the stream.
4. Repeat. Intermittently, `CopyToAsync` throws `InvalidOperationException: Reading is not allowed after reader was completed.`

The same scenario over a bidirectional stream (client writes, then FIN; server reads to the end) passes every time.

### Exceptions (if any)

```
System.InvalidOperationException: Reading is not allowed after reader was completed.
   at System.IO.Pipelines.ThrowHelper.ThrowInvalidOperationException_NoReadingAllowed()
   at System.IO.Pipelines.Pipe.ReadAsync(CancellationToken token)
   at System.IO.Pipelines.PipeReader.CopyToAsync(Stream destination, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
```

### .NET Version

11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148

### Anything else?

- Related WebTransport follow-ups: #42788. A separate interop issue: #70384.
- We hit this while proxying WebTransport sessions, where client unidirectional streams are forwarded. The forwarder sees the stream cut off, with no way to tell whether all the data arrived.

Issues.Title: Remember me isPersistent understanding
Issues.Body:
This is more of a question but its not enough of a question that i could post it up on stack overflow without risking it just getting closed as primary opinion based or to broad.   So i am going to put it here in hopes of getting an answer.

The issue is the understanding of how remember me is supposed to work.    My problem is that its not doing what we would expect it to do.   

Management expects when a user logs in and clicks remember me that they will then not be required to type their login and password again for a month.  Whether or not they will still have to type in the 2fa code is up for debate.

What is actually happening is that i can close the browser reboot and come back for about an hour and 15 minutes and then i will be forced to type my password again.    This still happens even with a valid `.AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie set that is not due to expire for another month.

After digging around in the code i found that Remember me is actually isPersistent and it is defined as.

>Flag indicating whether the sign-in cookie should persist after the browser is closed.

Which brings you to:

There are two different types of Cookies:

- session cookies, held in memory, and which expire once the browser exits
- persistent cookies, which have a time-to-live, are persisted on disk, and are sent by the browser until their time-to-live has elapsed.

All this being said remember machine 2fa works as expected i am not prompted again for the 2fa and i have a cookie on my machine `Identity.TwoFactorRememberMe`.

So I guess my question is why are we not getting a `Identity.FactorRememberMe` or why isn't sign in respecting a long life time of the `AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie?

How is this supposed to work exactly?   I am following the code here even though we have normal MVC and not razor pages like you have in the example.  I am still just calling 

>var signInUserResult = await _signInManager.PasswordSignInAsync(userName, password, rememberMe, true);

Note: I am using Asp .net Identity in Identity server 4 application.

Issues.Title: Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?
Issues.Body:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.identity.entityframeworkcore.identityuser?view=aspnetcore-1.1

I'm looking through various implementations from the [readme](https://github.com/aspnet/Identity/blob/master/README.md) and I've noticed they all use `IdentityUser ` for their concrete type to pass to `UserManager`, or have had to craft a custom type to be able to have a contract between the database and the .NET AspNetIdentity implentation they've written (see the DynamoDB library).

I've had to do this too for the [Marten implementation I've written](https://github.com/yetanotherchris/Marten.AspNetIdentity), and the reason is, a `TUser` that your `UserStore` takes, should really be an interface - it will always have an email, most likely an Id of some sort, firstname, lastname and then a bag of properties.

Things become even more abstract when dealing with claims.

If everyone is using `IdentityUser` or their own custom `TUser` doesn't this defeat the purpose of AspnetIdentity - which is to be able to switch and change implementations easily? That isn't possible if your consumer is tightly coupled with a `TUser` implementation of the library.

### Example `TUser` implementations

- [MongoIdentityUser](https://github.com/tugberkugurlu/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/MongoIdentityUser.cs)
- [DynamoIdentityUser](https://github.com/miltador/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/DynamoIdentityUser.cs)
- [Redis uses `IdentityUser<string>`](https://github.com/aguacongas/Identity.Redis/blob/develop/src/Aguacongas.Identity.Redis/UserStore.cs)
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?" (#2056)

I used to be able to use `dotnet watch` in Visual Studio by adding the following section to `launchSettings.json` and starting the project without debugging using CTRL + F5.

```
    "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    },
```

This used to work in ASP.NET Core 1.1 but no longer does. According to https://github.com/aspnet/DotNetTools/issues/404 the new format for ASP.NET Core 2.0 is:

```
   "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "workingDirectory": "C:\\Users\\namc\\source\\repos\\WebApplication2\\WebApplication2",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    }
```

The problem with this is the hard coded `executablePath` which is Windows specific and the `workingDirectory` which is specific to wherever I did a Git clone on my local machine.

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: OpenID Connect max_age validates auth_time
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the OpenID Connect handler validates the signed ID token `auth_time` claim whenever `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge` causes an effective `max_age` value to be sent.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69321 and addresses https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/67462.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

The handler sent `max_age` on the authorization request but did not validate the returned ID token's `auth_time`. Applications relied entirely on the identity provider to honor the request. A missing, malformed, stale, or excessively future `auth_time` did not cause authentication to fail.

### New behavior

When an effective `max_age` is sent, the handler correlates the exact value through protected authorization-transaction state and validates every ID token used by the supported authorization flow after normal token and OpenID Connect protocol validation.

The `auth_time` claim must be an integral, nonnegative OpenID Connect NumericDate. Authentication fails when the claim is missing, malformed, fractional, negative, overflowed, later than the current time plus `OpenIdConnectOptions.TokenValidationParameters.ClockSkew`, or older than `max_age` plus that clock skew. Exact boundaries and values within skew are accepted.

The validation covers authorization-code, implicit, and hybrid flows, including both relevant ID tokens in hybrid flows, and both the default `TokenHandler` path and legacy `SecurityTokenValidator` path. No validation occurs when no `max_age` is configured. In addition to the `MaxAge` properties, applications can configure the parameter through `AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` or `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

OpenID Connect Core requires the authorization server to include `auth_time` when `max_age` is requested and recommends that the relying party validate it. Correlating and checking the signed assertion prevents a missing or nonconforming assertion from silently satisfying an application's configured maximum authentication age.

The guarantee remains limited to the trusted identity provider's signed assertion. ASP.NET Core cannot prove that a particular physical authentication ceremony occurred and cannot protect against a compromised identity provider that signs false data. This change does not revalidate UserInfo, refresh-token redemption, local cookie lifetime, or physical user interaction.

### Recommended action

Ensure that identity providers emit a valid signed `auth_time` and honor the requested `max_age` whenever the application configures that parameter, most commonly through `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`.

For a temporarily incompatible provider, restore the previous request-only behavior by setting the process-wide compatibility switch before authentication starts:

```csharp
AppContext.SetSwitch(
    "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation",
    true);
```

The equivalent runtime configuration is:

```json
{
  "runtimeOptions": {
    "configProperties": {
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation": true
    }
  }
}
```

The switch defaults to `false` and is intended only as a temporary provider-compatibility escape hatch.

When pushed authorization is used, set or modify `max_age` in `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`. Changing it later in `OnPushAuthorization` is rejected while validation is active unless pushing is skipped, because the handler has already correlated the value with the authorization response.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. The behavioral change affects applications that set:

- `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectOptions.AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` when it includes `max_age`
- `OpenIdConnectEvents.OnRedirectToIdentityProvider` when it sets `max_age`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Identity external login keys use ordinal equality
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the built-in Entity Framework Core Identity stores verify external-login `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values using managed ordinal equality after the indexed database lookup returns a candidate.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69277.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

`UserStore` and `UserOnlyStore` filtered external logins with a database-translated equality predicate. The database collation therefore determined whether the stored `(LoginProvider, ProviderKey)` tuple matched the supplied values.

On a case-insensitive collation, `FindByLoginAsync` could resolve a login whose provider name or provider key differed only by case. On databases where equality ignores trailing spaces, it could also resolve a key that differed by trailing spaces. `RemoveLoginAsync` used the same collation-dependent lookup and could remove such a login.

### New behavior

The database equality remains the indexed candidate lookup. The built-in EF Identity stores then require the returned `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` to match the requested values using `StringComparison.Ordinal`.

A collation-only match now causes `FindByLoginAsync` to return no user and `RemoveLoginAsync` to perform no removal. Exact ordinal matches continue to work.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

External provider keys are opaque identifiers whose equality must not vary with the configured database provider or collation. Managed ordinal verification makes the built-in EF stores consistent with the in-memory reference store while preserving the existing indexed database lookup.

### Recommended action

Ensure that applications persist and later supply the exact `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values issued for an external login. Do not normalize, case-fold, trim, or otherwise alter provider keys.

Third-party `IUserLoginStore<TUser>` implementations own their equality semantics. Implementations that query a collation-aware database should preserve an indexed candidate lookup and verify the materialized provider name and key with ordinal equality before resolving or removing a login.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. This behavioral change affects the built-in Entity Framework Core implementations of:

- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.FindByLoginAsync`
- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.RemoveLoginAsync`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Blazor server-side rendering defers antiforgery validation to middleware
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, Blazor static server-side rendering (SSR) endpoints no longer validate antiforgery tokens themselves. They rely on the antiforgery verdict recorded by upstream middleware and generate antiforgery tokens only when token-based antiforgery middleware is present.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/67082.

### Version

.NET 11 Preview 6

### Previous behavior

When a Blazor SSR endpoint handled a form `POST`, the endpoint validated the request itself if antiforgery middleware hadn't already recorded a result.

The endpoint also generated and stored antiforgery tokens for rendered forms even when `app.UseAntiforgery()` wasn't present in the pipeline.

Consequently, apps that didn't call `app.UseAntiforgery()` still emitted and validated antiforgery tokens.

### New behavior

Blazor SSR endpoints now trust the `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature` verdict recorded by upstream middleware. A form `POST` is rejected with `400 Bad Request` when the recorded verdict is invalid.

The verdict can be recorded by:

- Token-based antiforgery middleware added by `app.UseAntiforgery()` (explicit usage).
- Automatic cross-origin CSRF protection middleware added by default to apps built with `WebApplication.CreateBuilder`.

Blazor SSR endpoints no longer call `IAntiforgery.ValidateRequestAsync` directly. Antiforgery tokens are generated only when token-based antiforgery middleware ran for the request.

Apps using `app.UseAntiforgery()` retain token-based validation. Apps without it rely on automatic cross-origin CSRF protection and no longer emit antiforgery tokens for their forms.


### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

# ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach end of support on April 13, 2027

> Update: The ASP.NET Core 2.3 end of support date was updated from April 7, 2027 to April 13, 2027 to align with the Microsoft servicing release cycles.

Today we are announcing that ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach **end of support on April 13, 2027**. After that date, Microsoft will no longer provide security patches, bug fixes, or technical support for ASP.NET Core 2.3.

This announcement provides the required 12 months of advance notice, as defined by the [Microsoft Support Lifecycle Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/lifecycle/faq/general-lifecycle#what-is-the-lifecycle-policy-for-tools-) for products classified as "Tools."

## Current support policy

ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages (latest patched version only) are currently [supported](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/platform/support/policy/aspnet#dotnet-core) on .NET Framework, following the support cycle for those .NET Framework versions. After April 13, 2027, this support will end regardless of the .NET Framework version in use.

Note that the [ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/platform/support/policy/aspnet/2.3-packages) include the Entity Framework 2.3 packages, which will end support on the same date.

## Impact of end of support

After ASP.NET Core 2.3 reaches end of support:

- No new security updates will be issued for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- Continuing to use an unsupported version may expose your applications to security vulnerabilities.
- Technical support will no longer be available for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- The ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages will be deprecated.

## Upgrade recommendation

We recommend upgrading to a [currently supported version of .NET](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet), such as .NET 10 (LTS).

To help with the upgrade process, we recommend using [GitHub Copilot modernization](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/porting/github-copilot-app-modernization/overview), which provides AI-powered assistance to help you analyze, plan, and execute your migration to a modern .NET version.

Issues.Title: Add automation to create docs tracking issues for breaking changes
Issues.Body:
Automates creation of documentation tracking issues in `dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs` when breaking change issues are opened or labeled in this repository.

## Implementation

**New workflow:** `.github/workflows/create-docs-issue.yaml`

- Triggers on `issues.opened` and `issues.labeled` events with "Breaking change" label
- Creates issue in docs repo with:
  - Title: `[Breaking Change] <original title>`
  - Body: Link to source issue, full context
  - Labels: `breaking-change`, `aspnet/Announcements`
- Posts comment on source issue with link to docs issue

## Duplicate Prevention

Multi-layer detection to handle race conditions and partial failures:
- Checks for existing bot comments in source issue
- Searches docs repo by title before creating
- Concurrency control keyed on issue number

## Error Handling

Separate try-catch blocks for each operation:
- Comment listing failures → proceed with search
- Search failures → proceed with creation (fail open to avoid missing docs)
- Comment posting failures → don't fail workflow (docs issue already created)
- Permission errors → explicit message about `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` requirement

## Setup Required

Configure `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` repository secret with `repo` scope for cross-repository issue creation. Falls back to `GITHUB_TOKEN` but will fail with clear error message.

## Security

Explicit minimal permissions: `issues: write`, `contents: read`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Deprecating WebHostBuilder,  IWebHost, and WebHost
Issues.Body:
### Description

`WebHostBuilder` was replaced by `HostBuilder` ([generic host](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder)) in 3.0 and we also added [`WebApplicationBuilder`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) in 6.0.

We are now marking `WebHostBuilder` as obsolete to encourage users to move on to the alternatives which is where future investments will occur, and we're also marking `IWebHost` and `WebHost` as deprecated to clean up other parts of the now obsolete web host story.

### Version

.NET 10 RC 1

### Previous behavior

```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

### New behavior

Using `WebHostBuilder` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR004**:
> warning ASPDEPR004: WebHostBuilder is deprecated in favor of HostBuilder and WebApplicationBuilder. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/004.

Using `IWebHost` or `WebHost` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR008**:
> warning ASPDEPR008: WebHost is obsolete. Use HostBuilder or WebApplicationBuilder instead. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/008.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [x] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [ ] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

We recommend the use of `HostBuilder` and `WebApplication` going forward over `WebHostBuilder` because they have all the features of `WebHostBuilder` and will be the focus of future investment.

### Recommended action

See https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/host/generic-host or https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/webapplication for more details on the different hosting models. As well as [HostBuilder replaces WebHostBuilder](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder) and [Introducing WebApplication](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) for migration guides.

Below is an example of converting `WebHostBuilder` to `HostBuilder`:

**Before**
```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

**After**
```csharp
using var host = new HostBuilder()
    .ConfigureWebHost(webHostBuilder =>
    {
        webHostBuilder
            .UseTestServer() // If using TestServer
            .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
            .UseStartup()
            .UseKestrel();
    })
    .Build();
await host.StartAsync();

var testServer = host.GetTestServer();
```

Both Copilot and ChatGpt have given good results so far when asked to convert a WebHostBuilder example to use HostBuilder. Below is an example prompt:
<details>
<summary>Example AI Prompt</summary>

> Can you convert
>
> var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
>     .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
>     .UseStartup()
>     .UseKestrel();
> // Test code might use TestServer:
> var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
>
> to use HostBuilder.

</details>

### Affected APIs

`public class Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.WebHostBuilder`
`public interface Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.IWebHost`
`public static class Microsoft.AspNetCore.WebHost`

### Discussion

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/63480

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Exception diagnostics are suppressed when `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns true
Issues.Body:
### Description

The [ASP.NET Core exception handler middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#exception-handler-page), `UseExceptionHandler()`, is responsible for catching and processing unhandled exceptions from ASP.NET Core requests.

In .NET 8, we introduced [`IExceptionHandler`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#iexceptionhandler). Implementations of `IExceptionHandler` are registered with dependency injection and invoked by the middleware. An implementation can return `true` from `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` to indicate that the exception has been handled. The middleware stops processing the exception once it has been handled.

In .NET 10, we're changing the default behavior so that the middleware no longer records diagnostics for exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

### Version

.NET 10 Preview 7

### Previous behavior

The exception handler middleware recorded diagnostics about exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

The exception diagnostics are:

- Logging `UnhandledException` to `ILogger`.
- Writing the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics.HandledException` event to `EventSource`.
- Adding the `error.type` tag to the `http.server.request.duration` metric.

### New behavior

If `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns `true`, then exception diagnostics are no longer recorded by default.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

ASP.NET Core users have given feedback that the previous behavior was undesirable. Their `IExceptionHandler` implementation reported that the exception was handled, but the error handling middleware still recorded the error in the app's telemetry.

We are changing ASP.NET Core to follow the behavior expected by users by suppressing diagnostics when `IExceptionHandler` handles the exception. We're also adding configuration options to customize exception diagnostics behavior if needed.

### Recommended action

If you want handled exceptions to continue recording telemetry, you can use the new `ExceptionHandlerOptions.SuppressDiagnosticsCallback` option:

```cs
app.UseExceptionHandler(new ExceptionHandlerOptions
{
    SuppressDiagnosticsCallback = context => false;
});
```

The context passed to the callback includes information about the exception, the request, and whether the exception was handled. Returning `false` from the callback indicates that diagnostics shouldn't be suppressed. This restores the previous behavior.

### References

- Issue: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/54554
- PR: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/59074

### Affected APIs

- `UseExceptionHandler()`
- `IExceptionHandler`
